episodes.title: Episode 1 – Solution Design & Architecture
episodes.intro: Welcome to episode one, Solution Design and Architecture. This domain is seventeen percent of the exam, one of the two heaviest. Across six parts we go from a vague business request to an architecture you can defend in front of a review committee: how Claude behaves and what that means for design, who owns each piece of work, which pattern fits, how multi-agent systems stay honest, how to break down a complex problem, and how to show the business why the system is worth building.

parts.narration:
### The four properties you design around

Before you decide what Claude should do in a solution, you need a clear picture of how Claude behaves. The training material frames this as four properties. None of them is a flaw to be fixed. Each is a force you design around, the way a structural engineer designs around the properties of steel or concrete. And for each one, the same characteristic that makes Claude capable in one situation makes it fail in another.

The first property is next-token prediction. Claude is excellent at tasks built on common patterns: summarising, reformatting, explaining well-established ideas. The limitation is precision on specifics. Claude can produce text that looks accurate but isn't, and that risk concentrates around names, dates, citations and statistics. The mitigation is citations, uncertainty signalling and generator-verifier loops, and routing specific factual lookups through tool calls or authoritative sources instead of trusting the model's output alone.

The second property is knowledge. Claude answers reliably on topics that are common, recent and consistently represented in its training data. It is unreliable on topics that are rare, niche, contested or frequently changing, and it presents stale information in the same confident tone it uses for established facts. The mitigation is to make an external system the source of truth, using web search, retrieval, tool use or MCP servers. When freshness or authority matters, you re-introduce the data yourself.

The third property is working memory. Anything that fits in the active context window is available. The window is a hard edge: once content falls outside it, the model has no access at all. Two different errors happen at that edge, and they are easy to confuse. An oversized request is rejected before generation. If the prompt exceeds the model's token limit, the API returns a 400 invalid request error saying the prompt is too long. If the raw request body exceeds the byte limit, the API returns a 413 request too large error. The other error is when the prompt fits, but generation runs into the window ceiling and stops early; on current models the response comes back with a model context window exceeded stop reason and truncated output. To stay clear of the edge, check the usage field on every response and use the token-counting API before you send. The design mitigations are progressive context loading, chunking, front-loading critical information, and summarising across turns.

The fourth property is steerability. Claude follows short, concrete, verifiable instructions well: defined formats, explicit length limits, clear roles. It struggles with abstract or ambiguous instructions, long reasoning chains, and precise numerical or logical computation, and it can follow the letter of an instruction while drifting from the intent. For high-stakes numerical accuracy, deterministic computation or tool execution should own the answer. Use system prompts, structured outputs and code execution, and restate the goal alongside the instruction.

### From property to design consequence

Map these properties to four design consequences now, because they feed every later decision. Non-determinism: the same input can produce different outputs across runs, which is why evaluation frameworks exist. You cannot certify behaviour you only observed once. Context as a finite resource: what you put in the window, in what order, and what you leave out are design decisions that affect quality and cost. Confidence is not validity: Claude can be wrong in the same fluent, assured tone it uses when it is right, which is why human review and verification are architectural choices rather than afterthoughts. And knowledge and capability boundaries: for rare, private or fast-changing topics, an external system must be the source of truth.

The course gives a sharp example. An architect saw a demo run cleanly five times in a row and concluded the behaviour was deterministic. The team shipped a financial reconciliation pipeline with no checks around the model output. In week two, the same statement, re-processed, produced a different categorisation, and it was found only because an analyst happened to re-run a batch. The lesson is not that the model is unreliable. It is that a demo is not evidence of determinism, and the four properties are present whether your architecture acknowledges them or not. The cost of ignoring them lands after launch, when rework is most expensive, and the failure doesn't announce itself. The system drifts quietly until an audit or an angry user finds it.

### Claude, systems and humans

Now the translation move. A partner rarely hands you a clean requirement. They say something like, we want AI to handle our claims. Your first job is to split that into separate capabilities and give each one an owner. Every solution has three owners. Claude takes the work that benefits from language understanding, summarisation, planning, drafting or tool-mediated action. Existing systems keep anything the partner has already paid to make reliable: the order-status service, the policy engine, the rules table, the database of record. Humans keep the judgement calls, the exception paths, the approvals, and the moments where being right matters more than being fast. Over-assigning work to Claude is the most common and most expensive early mistake. It almost always makes the process more expensive, slower and harder to govern.

### The scoping sequence

Module two turns this into a four-step scoping sequence. Step one: business requirement to capability list. Process insurance claims is a goal, not a capability. The capabilities might be extracting structured fields from the claim, looking up coverage in the policy database, routing the claim to an adjuster queue by type and value, and drafting the adjuster notification. Step two: capability list to architecture sketch, deciding for each capability whether Claude, an existing system or a human owns it. Step three: architecture sketch to boundary conditions. State where the architecture works and where it doesn't. A design that works for documents up to twenty pages but fails beyond that has a boundary condition that must be written down. Step four: boundary conditions into the statement of work, so the build team and the business owner agree on what is in scope and what is explicitly out.

### Technical feasibility and the three verdicts

A feasibility assessment that only asks can Claude do this is a capability check. Run each capability through the four properties instead. Does the task need probabilistic generation, or precision on specific values like account numbers and claim amounts? Does it depend on rare or recent knowledge that must be brought into context? Do the inputs fit the window, or does the task need chunking or a pipeline? Are the instructions concrete and verifiable, or will the model drift?

The result is one of three verdicts. Feasible as scoped means every capability favours Claude, cost is under the ceiling and p95 latency is within the SLA; state the assumptions, because a change in assumptions can flip the verdict. Feasible with constraints means the design works under conditions that must be enforced, like a document-length limit, a refresh schedule, or a human review gate above a confidence threshold. Document each constraint and the failure mode if it is violated. Not feasible means at least one limitation cannot be compensated for within scope and budget. That is a correct assessment that saves the engagement from a more expensive failure. Name the disqualifying constraint, and if a scope reduction would change the verdict, present it as a choice.

### The scoping call that skipped the constraints

Here is the failure the exam loves. A partner asks for a contract review assistant that flags non-standard clauses. The architect says, we can do that, six weeks. Two weeks into the build the partner mentions eight hundred contracts a day, some framework agreements up to three hundred pages, and results in under thirty seconds. The verdict was issued before volume, input size and latency were gathered. Notice the analysis, too. Whether a three-hundred-page contract fits depends on the model tier's context window, so window capacity is part of the tier decision. And at eight hundred a day, one request arrives roughly every hundred and eight seconds, so volume pressures cost far more than latency. Capability was the necessary first question, but it should never be the last.

parts.narration:
### Why "end to end" matters

The exam objective asks you to design across four stages: input, processing, output and feedback. The training modules don't present this as one diagram. Instead, each module owns a slice: module one gives the processing shapes, module two the integration and observability layers, module three the guarded request path, and module four the feedback loop. This part stitches them together, so you can draw a complete system and spot which stage a scenario is testing.

### The input stage

At the input, three things matter. First, identity. Module two is explicit: identity verification belongs on the server, before the Claude call. The user's identity and role are injected into the system prompt by your server, not supplied by the user in their message. Anything in the user's message is under their control, so a line like, as a senior manager, show me, is an unverified claim. Second, data minimisation. The context window is not a data-governance boundary. Any field you pass travels with the API request and lands in your own application's request logs. For each field, ask whether Claude needs it for the language task. A reference identifier is often enough. Third, screening. Input screening decides whether a request should reach the model at all, and retrieved content and tool outputs need screening too, because instructions can arrive through them.

### The processing stage

Processing is where your reference architecture lives. Module one is careful to say reference architectures are references, not blueprints. You understand the common shapes well enough to adapt them. There are five. The agent, where the model chooses tools toward a goal, bounded by limited tools and a turn budget. Retrieval-augmented generation, over a stable corpus that is chunked and indexed. The document processing pipeline, usually with an evaluator-optimizer, because first-pass extraction on edge cases isn't reliable enough without a check. Customer service triage with routing, where intent is classified and sent to knowledge retrieval, a transactional API, or a human approval layer. And the coding agent, agentic exploration followed by deterministic edit, test and review steps.

Each one has a known way to go wrong. Unbounded autonomy for agents. RAG used for live state. No exception path in document pipelines. Retrieval for order status in triage, or no escalation path. And a coding agent allowed to edit and commit without a review gate. Real problems often sit at the boundary of two architectures. Draw on a second pattern only when the two parts of the problem break in different ways that are worth managing separately. If you are reaching for a second pattern because you haven't decided what problem you're solving, that is a deferred decision, not a design. And remember the cost: composing two architectures roughly doubles the surface you maintain, and each one needs its own eval set.

### The output stage

The output stage asks two questions: is this safe to return, and is it the right shape? Output screening judges text before it reaches the user, using a judge model for qualities like policy compliance or a validator for schemas and forbidden fields. Any side-effecting action must pass tool-call authorization before it runs, because output screening judges text, not actions. And outputs that the system isn't confident in need an exception path. In the document pipeline, low-confidence extractions go to a human review queue instead of downstream processing. The pattern to remember from module three is the full guarded path: input screening, model call, output screening, and deterministic authorization before any side effect, with every blocked or failed gate logged.

### The feedback stage

This is the stage most diagrams leave out. A design that ends at response to user cannot notice that it is getting worse. Module two tells you what to log on every request: the request itself, with model version, input tokens and prompt identifier; the response, with output tokens, latency and stop reason; the context, with user role, session ID and whether caching applied; and the outcome, whether the downstream system accepted the output. Module four adds the decision layer on top. Observability collects signals, but a feedback loop maps each signal to a trigger, an owner and an action: signals, triage, decide, act, review. And corrections become data. When a reviewer fixes an extraction, that correction can feed the golden dataset, so the next eval run measures the system against what production actually taught you.

### Reliability belongs in the design too

Module two adds three reliability controls that sit at different layers. Retries with exponential backoff sit close to the API call, for transient errors like 429 rate limits, timeouts and 5xx responses. Circuit breakers sit at the service boundary and trip when a dependency's error rate crosses a threshold, so requests fail fast instead of waiting. Fallback chains sit in the orchestration layer and route to an alternative model tier or a cached response instead of surfacing an error. Put them in the wrong layer and you protect the wrong part of the system. Add model version pinning to every architecture, with a version-update runbook, because an unpinned version can roll forward without re-validation.

### Putting it together

Picture invoice processing. Input: OCR, a tenant ID injected server-side, only the fields the extraction needs. Processing: schema-bound extraction with an evaluator pass. Output: validated JSON, with low-confidence fields routed to a reviewer. Feedback: traces with model version, tokens and stop reason, an acceptance signal from the finance system, reviewer corrections flowing into the golden dataset, and a quality-drift trigger owned by a named person. When an exam scenario describes a system that works but quietly degrades, the missing piece is almost always that last stage.

parts.narration:
### Three patterns on two axes

Once you know which parts of a task Claude owns, the next decision is structural: what shape does Claude's involvement take? Module one gives three patterns, and places each on two axes. The first axis is predictability, how predictable the path through the work is. The second is model autonomy, how much decision-making you are willing to hand to the model.

The augmented LLM is a single model invocation. You send the request, the model completes the task, and your code handles the wiring. You can add tool use, retrieval or extended thinking to that call, but the model does one bounded job in one pass, and the control flow never branches on what the model decides. It sits in the high-predictability, low-autonomy corner. Use it when the task is well defined, the output is verifiable, and there's no reason to split the work.

A workflow decomposes the task into named steps orchestrated in your own code. Each step may or may not call Claude. Because control flow lives in your code, you can log it, test it and reason about it like any other software. Workflows occupy the middle band: the overall shape is predictable, and each step may involve contained model judgement. Use one when error cost is real, observability matters and the steps can be determined in advance.

An agent gets a goal and a set of tools, and the model decides its own sequence of steps. The control flow lives inside the model. That's what makes it an agent: the path is not written anywhere you can inspect in advance. Use it only when the path cannot be enumerated in advance, and only when an unexpected or inconsistent output is acceptable and recoverable. Claude Code is the production example: it explores an unfamiliar codebase, decides which files to read based on what it found, and runs multi-step work no one could script. In production, agents are bound by constrained tool entry points, per-turn budgets, explicit permissions and stopping criteria. Module one is firm that these constraints are not optional.

### Workflow sub-patterns

Choosing a workflow doesn't fully specify the design. The module notes four workflow shapes; the guide uses Anthropic's names for them: prompt chaining, where steps run in sequence; routing, where an input is classified and sent to a specialised path; parallelisation, where independent pieces run at the same time; and evaluator-optimizer, where one pass generates and another critiques. They aren't mutually exclusive, and most production workflows combine them. The rule is to pick the simplest shape that meets error tolerance and observability requirements, then revisit with production data and escalate only when measurement shows the simpler pattern falling short.

### The five deciding factors

Walk five factors in sequence: predictability, error cost, observability, latency and cost. For each, ask whether it rules out any pattern. The first factor that rules one out is the deciding one, and the tightest constraint decides. When error cost is the binding constraint, error cost picks the pattern. Two cautions from the module. Agents don't automatically cost more than workflows; what drives cost is how much context accumulates and how many model calls are made, so a poorly designed workflow can cost more than a well-designed agent. And workflows and agents fail differently: a workflow fails when a step in your code fails, while an agent fails when the model makes a bad decision somewhere across many turns, which is harder to see and harder to debug. An agent's autonomy is your liability surface, because it can do anything its tools allow, including combinations nobody tested.

### When the team wanted flexibility and got non-determinism

The module's retrospective case has three quotes. One: we picked an agent because we didn't want to constrain it too early, and by month two we'd added so many guardrail tools we'd basically rewritten the workflow inside the agent loop, minus the logging. Two: compliance asked which step approved a disbursement; we pointed at a model turn; they asked which version of the model; the version had rolled forward two weeks earlier and nobody had re-validated. Three: when we mined the traces, the paths fell into only four shapes; we could have written a router and four chains and saved six months.

Read the failures carefully, because the exam does. The team optimised for imagined future flexibility instead of the known present shape. Non-determinism became a compliance problem, because there was no discrete, auditable step to point to. And the unpinned model version was a separate model-governance gap that would have hurt a workflow just as much. Only one of those two compliance failures is about the agent pattern itself. Choosing an agent when you're unsure is not a safe default. If the work had been genuinely unpredictable, the agent would have been the right call for exactly that reason.

### Try prompting before fine-tuning

When prompting feels unreliable, the instinct is fine-tuning. On Claude that's usually the wrong first move. Optimise the prompt, because most reliability problems are prompt problems. Then add tool use or retrieval. Then move to a stronger pattern like evaluator-optimizer. Only then consider fine-tuning, and only for very high volume where inference cost is the real constraint, critical latency where a smaller specialised model wins, or a consistent output format that prompting hasn't solved. Fine-tuning locks you to a model version and narrows your options. The module also notes that fine-tuning Claude is not broadly available, so confirm options with the Anthropic account team before recommending it.

### Packaging and delegation

Alongside the pattern, decide the packaging: a prompt-only solution, direct tool use, or a Skills-based architecture, where a versioned Skill packages the procedure, instructions and scripts as one governed unit. Reach for a Skill when the same procedure runs repeatedly, is distributed across teams or products, or must be versioned and governed. Finally, apply the delegation lens to the pattern itself: does this pattern grant Claude appropriate or excessive decision authority for the risk in front of you? Autonomy is justified only when the stakes and reversibility of the agent's actions support it.

parts.narration:
### When one agent isn't enough

Pattern selection tells you when to reach for an agent. Some problems are too large or too varied for a single agent to hold in one context. Then the design moves to multiple agents working together. Module one keeps the vocabulary simple: there are two roles.

The orchestrator owns the goal. It decomposes the work, decides what to delegate, and synthesises the results into a single answer. It never does the sub-task work itself; its job is delegation and synthesis. The subagents own scoped sub-tasks. Each runs in its own context, does one piece, and returns a result.

Three things must be designed rather than assumed. How the work is decomposed into sub-tasks. How each subagent's result is structured so the orchestrator can combine it. And how the orchestrator resolves conflicts or gaps when results come back.

### The fan-out pattern

The most common multi-agent shape is a fan-out. A parent agent faces a work item too big for one context: a four-hundred-file codebase to audit, a two-hundred-document corpus to summarise, a regulatory filing to check against fifty rules. The orchestrator splits the item into independent units, dispatches one subagent per unit, in parallel where the units don't depend on each other, and then synthesises the returned results. The win is twofold. Each subagent works in a clean context sized to its unit, and independent units run at the same time.

### Where a failure can be caught

The architectural question to ask is where each failure mode is recoverable. A subagent failure is usually recoverable: the orchestrator can retry the unit, route it elsewhere, or drop it and flag the gap while the rest of the work proceeds. An orchestrator failure usually is not: if the agent that owns the goal and holds the synthesis loses its thread, the whole run fails and partial subagent work may be stranded. So design for the asymmetry. Make subagent work idempotent and retryable, and protect the orchestrator's state.

Module one gives four failure rows to remember. A subagent returns a malformed or empty result: validate each result, retry or re-route the unit, and record the gap rather than failing the run. Two subagents return conflicting results: give the orchestrator an explicit conflict-resolution rule, or escalate the conflict to a human. The orchestrator loses its goal or synthesis state: protect that state and checkpoint progress so a failed run can resume rather than restart. Traces fragment across orchestrator and subagents: propagate a shared trace identifier so one run can be reconstructed end to end. Module two repeats this in its failure-mode table for orchestrator-workers, and adds that attribution later depends on a trace spanning both levels.

### When fan-out hid a dropped unit

Here is the case you must know. A compliance team checked a fifty-section vendor contract against an internal policy checklist. The orchestrator fanned out one subagent per section, each returning pass or flag, and produced a clean summary: forty-eight sections reviewed, three flagged. It went to the legal lead. Two sections had never been reviewed. One subagent timed out and returned nothing. Another failed to parse a scanned page and returned an empty result. The orchestrator counted only what it received.

Three gaps lined up. The count was never reconciled: no rule said results returned must equal units dispatched. A recoverable failure had nothing watching it: a timeout and an empty parse are both the recoverable case, but only if something retries or flags them. And the output read as complete: fluent and well-formed, which is exactly what hid the gap. The fix is a coverage check at synthesis. Results returned must equal units dispatched, or the run flags the difference before anyone reads the summary.

### Trust boundaries between agents

Module two adds least privilege to multi-agent design. Every tool you connect is an attack surface and a cost. In an orchestrator-worker deployment, establish the trust hierarchy by scoping each subagent's tool access to its task, so a subagent can't reach tools its job doesn't need. A summarising subagent has no business holding a write tool.

### Where humans belong

A multi-agent system can take many actions before a human sees anything, so checkpoint placement is a deliberate design choice. A human-in-the-loop checkpoint is a gate that pauses execution for review, positioned by the risk and reversibility of the action about to happen. Place a gate before any irreversible or high-stakes action a subagent would otherwise take on its own. Sample lower-stakes actions instead of gating each one. The gate is part of the orchestration design, not bolted on afterwards.

### Cost and complexity

Multi-agent systems multiply token spend: every subagent has its own context, and the orchestrator pays to synthesise. Reach for the pattern when the work genuinely exceeds one context, not as a default. Each added agent is another failure boundary to observe and govern, so the discipline is the fewest agents that meet the requirement, with clear ownership of the goal. And the dangerous failure is the silent one, a subagent that drops a unit under a confident synthesis.

parts.narration:
### Two kinds of decomposition

The word decomposition shows up in two places in the course, and the exam expects you to use both. The first is decomposition by owner: splitting a partner's request into what Claude does, what existing systems do, and what humans do. The second is decomposition by unit of work: splitting a large task into pieces that fit a context, can run independently, and come back in a shape you can combine. Good designs do the first before the second.

### Decomposition by owner: the delegation map

Module one calls the output of owner decomposition a delegation map. For each part of the request you decide not just whether Claude can do it, but whether Claude should own it. Each part lands in one of three categories: AI-appropriate work, human-retained work, or collaborative work where Claude drafts and a person decides. Justify every assignment through three questions. Reversibility: can a wrong call be undone? Stakes: what does a wrong call cost? Accountability: who must answer for it? Delegation is the first of the four AI Fluency competencies the course uses, and this is where you apply it.

The four properties tell you what Claude can be trusted with. Language work, summarising, classification and drafting suit Claude. Authoritative values and arithmetic suit deterministic systems, because next-token prediction is weak on specifics and steerability is weak on precise computation. Live state belongs to the system of record, reached by a tool call. And approvals and exceptions stay with people, because confidence is not validity.

### Decomposition by unit of work

For large tasks, the second decomposition kicks in. Module two's scoping sequence starts it: turn the business requirement into a capability list, naming each capability separately so you can assign it. Then, where a capability is too big for one call, split it into units. Good units are independent, so they can run in parallel without waiting on each other. They are sized to a clean context. And they return a structured result, so the orchestrator or the next step can combine them without guessing. Record the count of units dispatched, because synthesis must reconcile it.

The boundary conditions come out of this step. If a unit is defined as one contract section and some sections are scanned images, that's a constraint. If the design works up to a page count, that's a boundary condition for the statement of work. Decomposition is also where you discover that some capability should never have been Claude's at all.

### A worked decomposition: the law-firm brief

Module one closes with an assembly exercise. A hundred-and-eighty-lawyer firm wants to speed up contract review. Senior associates spend twelve to eighteen hours a week reading thirty-five-page vendor contracts against the firm's playbook. Documents live in iManage, there is a CIO-approved private LLM gateway, and attorney-client privilege rules out consumer-grade tools. The target is sixty percent less associate time per contract, with the senior associate still the final reviewer.

Here's the model answer, decomposed. The entry point is the direct API or SDK in a thin internal web app with the firm's SSO, routed through the approved gateway. The pattern is a parallelised workflow, reviewing the contract section by section, with an evaluator pass enforcing a strict schema on the flagged-clauses output. Claude owns extraction, classification against the playbook, and draft redlines. Existing systems own the rest: the playbook stays a versioned source of truth retrieved per clause at call time, and iManage handles document fetch. Model and context: Sonnet as the default with progressive context, and extended thinking per clause only where an eval justifies it. Humans: the senior associate signs off on every output, and low-confidence clauses are flagged for attention.

Notice what each wrong option in that exercise gets wrong. Each one looks reasonable but fails on a single decision, for example a consumer entry point that privilege rules out, or a design where Claude holds the playbook in its head instead of retrieving the versioned source.

### The cost of getting decomposition wrong

Designs that skip owner decomposition force Claude into work another system would do more cheaply and reliably, or ask it to work without the context a human would have given a colleague. Designs that skip unit decomposition hit the working-memory cliff, or produce one huge call that can't be retried in pieces. Both show up later as cost overruns, unexplained errors or audit findings. Decomposition is cheap at the whiteboard and expensive after launch.

parts.narration:
### Feasible is not the same as worth building

A feasibility verdict tells the business owner the system can be built within budget and constraints. It doesn't say whether building it is worth doing. Business value and ROI mapping answer that second question, and they connect your architecture to outcomes the business already tracks: hours saved, error rates reduced, cycle time shortened, revenue protected. The mapping turns a technical design into a decision a budget holder can defend.

### The five pillars

Module two names five pillars, and the exam guide uses the same list. Efficiency: the same work done faster or cheaper. Transformation: work that wasn't feasible before becoming possible. Productivity: more output from the same people. Solution cost: the run cost of the system itself. And performance SLAs: the service levels the deployment must hold. Map each ROI claim to the pillar it advances, so the value statement says both the number and the kind of value it represents. A claim that sounds like efficiency but is really transformation needs a different baseline, because there was no prior process to compare against.

### Two states and a difference

The mechanism is a comparison between two states. The baseline is how the work is done today, measured in the unit the business cares about. The projected state is how the work is done once Claude is in the workflow, measured in the same unit. Value is the difference between them, minus the cost of running the system. That run cost comes straight from the sizing model you built earlier, so ROI reuses work you already did.

### The four steps

Step one: name the baseline in a business unit. For claims review, that might be analyst hours per claim or average days to resolution. The baseline must come from the business owner's own operational data, because every later number is compared to it. A baseline from intuition produces an ROI figure no finance team will accept.

Step two: predict the post-deployment state in the same unit. If the feasibility verdict needs human review, the projection must include it. Routing low-confidence output to a reviewer reduces labour, but it doesn't eliminate it. Projecting full automation when the design has a review gate overstates the value, and operations will reject the number.

Step three: subtract the run cost from the sizing model. This step isolates recurring run cost only. Build cost is handled in the payback calculation. Reusing the sizing output keeps the analyses consistent, so a change to token budget or model tier updates both the cost ceiling and the value case together.

Step four: state the payback period and the sensitivity. Payback is the time for accumulated gain to cover the build cost and the run cost. Then say how that period moves if volume or gain-per-task assumptions are wrong. Quoting payback without sensitivity invites a decision based on one optimistic scenario.

### The three ROI errors

Module two lists three common errors. The baseline is estimated rather than measured, which stays hidden until finance asks where the number came from, and then the whole case is rebuilt. The projection assumes full automation when the design requires human review, which surfaces in the first operational period when analyst hours don't fall as promised. And the run cost is taken from an average instead of the sizing distribution, which understates cost and overstates value, especially for heavy-tailed workloads where a small fraction of large requests drives most of the spend.

### The outcome document

Module four closes the loop after deployment with the customer outcome document. It has six fields: the use case with its scope boundary, the metric before, the metric after on the same definition, the control that makes the comparison auditable, the measurement owner after the engagement closes, and the reuse potential. Its cautionary case is memorable. An architect wrote the outcome document from what was easy to export: forty thousand requests a month, sub-two-second latency, an error rate under half a percent. The sponsor took it to the CFO, who asked what the deployment had done for the business: what were claim processing times before, and what are they now? The document had no answer. Without the before number there's no story, and without the control the after number is just an assertion. Capture the baseline at the start, so the value case can be proven at the end.

parts.narration:
### The three tiers

Module one describes the Claude model family as three tiers, each optimised for a different balance of cost, latency and capability. Opus is the most capable, suited to demanding reasoning, advanced coding and research synthesis where Sonnet doesn't meet your quality bar. Sonnet balances intelligence, speed and cost for most production work. Haiku is the fastest and cheapest.

The default starting point is Sonnet. Move up to Opus only when an eval set tells you Sonnet isn't meeting your quality bar. Move down to Haiku only when an eval set confirms the quality trade-off is acceptable for your specific task. The module is emphatic that the decision to move should be measured, not reflexive.

### Every model change is a release

Any change to the model is a change to the system's behaviour, so a swap between two models is a deployment and should be treated as one. At minimum you need three things. A curated test set of prompts with known-good outputs, covering the real distribution of work the system sees. A grading function, either model-graded against a rubric or programmatic where you can express the check in code. And a delta threshold, set in advance, below which you do not ship. Set the threshold before you run the eval. If you set it after, you aren't setting a standard. You're writing the acceptance criteria after the build.

### The worked downgrade

The module walks a downgrade that was done well. A document-intelligence pipeline has run on Sonnet for six months and used its whole budget. The team wants Haiku. They build two hundred and fifty representative documents with hand-validated extraction targets, stratified by document type, and sized so per-type scores stay meaningful, not just the average. Sonnet scores 0.94 on average; Haiku scores 0.86. The variance sits in two document types, at 0.71 and 0.74. The rollback criterion, set in advance, said that if any single document type drops below 0.85, the migration is rejected. Two crossed the line, so the migration as proposed is rejected. The salvage is a partial migration: route those two types to Sonnet through the existing classifier and the rest to Haiku. Cost drops without taking the regression. The lesson isn't the scores. It's that the criterion was fixed before the data came in, so the team didn't negotiate with itself, and the per-category view surfaced an option a single average would have hidden.

### The cost of not choosing

The second case is the opposite. When the demo has to land, use the best model sounds smart and needs no eval. Ninety days after launch, monthly cost was seven times the model, median latency was 2.3 seconds against an 800-millisecond target, and customer satisfaction hadn't moved. Every call used Opus. There was no per-step model selection, because there was no per-step eval to justify one. Cost was reviewed monthly, so the gap surfaced weeks after launch. And extended thinking had been switched on for a routing classifier that needed no reasoning at all. The fix: build the eval set retroactively, route the classifier to Haiku, route mid-pipeline summarisation to Sonnet, and keep Opus only on final response composition, where the eval said it earned its place. Cost fell seventy-one percent, median latency fell to 940 milliseconds, and satisfaction held. Remember the line: not choosing a model is equivalent to choosing the most expensive one. The eval set isn't just a release gate. It's the only thing that makes the tier decision defensible during design.

### Extended thinking

Extended thinking lets the model work through a problem in a separate block of thinking tokens before the final answer. Module one explains how the control has changed. On Claude Opus 4.6 and later, Sonnet 4.6 and later, and Sonnet 5, adaptive thinking with the effort parameter is the recommended control: you set how much reasoning effort to apply rather than a token budget. Adaptive thinking is the only mode on Claude Fable 5. The older budget tokens setting is deprecated on the 4.6 generation and removed on Sonnet 5, where it returns a 400. The module itself tells you to verify current support at publish time. Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens and add latency. When thinking isn't engaged, none are generated or billed. The API may return a summarised view of the reasoning, but you are billed for the thinking tokens actually used, not the length of the summary. The rule: run evals without it first, work on the prompt, and enable thinking only for a measured accuracy gap. It can't hurt is not evidence.

### Context window as part of the tier decision

Module two's scoping case adds one more dimension. Whether a three-hundred-page contract fits in one call depends on the tier's context window. A one-million-token window can take it without chunking; a two-hundred-thousand-token window may need a chunking strategy for the longest documents. So context capacity is part of the tier decision, not a settled assumption.

### Pin the version

Finally, model version pinning applies to every architecture. Pin versions in configuration, watch the deprecation page, and keep a version-update runbook. The ninety-day retrospective in episode one showed what happens otherwise: an auditor asked which version approved a disbursement, and it had rolled forward two weeks earlier without re-validation.

parts.narration:
### From sentence to asset

At enterprise scale, a prompt isn't a sentence you type. Module one calls it an asset you design: a system prompt, a reusable template, and the guardrails that keep both safe and consistent. A system prompt for a one-off chat and a system prompt that hundreds of requests a day depend on are different artifacts. When a prompt is reused at scale, ambiguity becomes a defect multiplied across every request.

### The structure of an enterprise system prompt

The enterprise version has structure. A clear statement of role and scope. The constraints the model must hold, meaning what it must never do and what it must always do. And an output contract, naming the exact shape the response must take. Those three pieces are what let you test the prompt, review it, and know when a change has broken it.

### Templates: the safe path as the default path

A template is a system prompt with parameterised slots, the parts that change per request, and fixed scaffolding around them. The design goal is that the fixed scaffolding carries the consistency and safety guarantees, so that filling a slot can't accidentally remove a constraint. A well-designed template makes the safe path the default path. The person using it supplies the variable content and inherits the guardrails without having to re-author them. Templates also concentrate complexity in one place where it can be reviewed and governed, instead of scattering it across ad-hoc prompts that nobody owns.

### Description: say what you mean

Description is one of the four AI Fluency competencies, the discipline of telling the model precisely what you want. Applied to prompt design, a well-described prompt names three things. The scope: what's in bounds and what's out. The format: the exact output contract. And the constraints: the rules that must never be violated. The failure to watch for is underspecification. It's a gap the model fills with its own assumption, and it fills it differently each time. That's exactly the non-determinism you don't want in a reused asset.

### Diagnosing underspecification

The architect's skill here is reading a prompt for what it fails to say. For each requirement the output must meet, ask whether the prompt actually states it, or merely hopes for it. Where the prompt is silent, the model improvises. The fix is to make the implicit explicit: restate the goal alongside the instruction, name the format, and bound the constraints. This connects back to steerability from episode one. Claude follows concrete, verifiable instructions well, and drifts on abstract ones.

### Structural guardrails beat stated ones

Module one's exercise is worth rehearsing. A support organisation drafts replies hundreds of times a day from a ticket and a manual section. Replies must follow tone guidelines, cite the manual section used, and never promise a refund or timeline the agent hasn't approved. Three decisions. First, the cache breakpoint: role, tone rules, output contract and the never-promise rule go first as the stable prefix; the ticket and the manual section are the only per-request content. Second, the guardrail: build it into the output contract as a structural constraint the format requires, not a sentence in the role text. A rule stated in the role can be drifted past; a constraint built into the output contract shapes the response format and can't be quietly ignored. Third, packaging: a versioned Skill, because the procedure is stable, runs identically across the support org, and needs versioning and rollback. A pasted template each agent keeps locally drifts into slightly different versions.

### Instructions are not enforcement

Module three adds the boundary you must respect. The system prompt is one layer in the safety stack. It reliably covers role, tone and stated constraints inside one request. It doesn't cover anything an adversarial or unusual input can talk Claude out of, because instructions are not enforcement. So system instructions shape behaviour, but deployment-specific policy is enforced only when those instructions are paired with runtime controls: screening, authorisation and review. And the risk callout from module one bears repeating. An underspecified guardrail is worse than a missing one, because it creates the appearance of a control without the substance. A constraint the model can quietly route around is not a constraint.

### The economics

A vague system prompt is paid for in every request that needs correction, retry or human clean-up. Designing it well once is far cheaper than diagnosing drift across thousands of calls.

parts.narration:
### Technique follows task complexity

Once a prompt is designed for reuse, the next question is which technique to use inside it. Module one is clear that the technique is chosen by the complexity of the task, not by habit. There are three main techniques.

Zero-shot means instruction only, with no examples. It fits well-specified tasks the model already handles reliably, and it's the default to try first.

Few-shot means a handful of input and output examples in the prompt. It fits tasks where the desired format or judgement is easier to show than to describe. If you find yourself writing three paragraphs explaining a tone, two good examples might do it better.

Chain-of-thought means prompting the model to reason step by step before it answers. It fits multi-step reasoning, arithmetic-like logic, or tasks where the path matters to the answer.

### The deliberate progression

The progression is deliberate. Start zero-shot. Add examples only if the task needs them. Add explicit reasoning only if the task's structure demands it. Each step adds tokens and latency, so reach for the lightest technique that meets the requirement. The cost callout in the module puts it bluntly: chain-of-thought on a task that doesn't need it is a recurring tax for no gain. And this sits inside the bigger sequence from episode one: optimise the prompt, then add tools or retrieval, then a stronger pattern like evaluator-optimizer, and only then consider fine-tuning.

How do you know which step you need? The same way you know anything in this course: measure. Run the zero-shot version against your eval set. If it meets the threshold, stop. If it fails in a pattern, say, wrong output shape, try a few examples. If it fails on tasks with several dependent steps, try explicit reasoning. Each move should be tied to a failure you observed.

### Same prompt, different model

The same prompt doesn't behave identically across model tiers or generations. A more capable model may need less scaffolding, fewer examples and less step-by-step instruction, to reach the same quality. A less capable model may need more. So a prompt tuned for one model is a starting point for another, not a finished artifact. This is why a model swap is gated with an eval: the prompt-and-model pairing is what you're actually shipping. If a team swaps Sonnet for Haiku and keeps the prompt unchanged, the eval may reveal that Haiku needs an extra example or a tighter output contract.

### Bias can be built into the prompt

Prompt construction can introduce bias the task never intended. The module names three sources. Leading phrasing that suggests an answer. Unbalanced examples, few-shot sets that show only one kind of case. And assumptions baked into the instruction itself. All of them steer output in ways that are easy to miss. The discipline is to phrase neutrally, balance examples across the cases the system will actually see, and check whether the prompt presumes an answer it should be eliciting. The risk is that bias introduced in the prompt is invisible in any single output and only shows up in aggregate. That's why neutral phrasing and balanced examples are a design requirement, not a polish step. You'll meet this again in episode five, where prompt framing and few-shot examples are two of the four places unequal outcomes can enter a system.

### Examples are content to maintain

Few-shot examples come with a maintenance cost. As the task evolves, stale examples quietly steer the model in the wrong direction. Treat them like code: version them, review them when the task changes, and include them in what the eval covers.

### Steerability ties it together

This all traces back to the steerability property. Claude does well with short, concrete, verifiable instructions with defined formats and clear roles. It drifts on abstract instructions, long reasoning chains and precise computation. So the technique choice is a steerability decision. Be concrete first. Show, if describing fails. Ask for reasoning when the path matters. And for precise arithmetic, don't prompt harder: let code or a tool compute the answer.

parts.narration:
### Four terms that get conflated

Module one starts this topic with four terms that are often used interchangeably, and conflating them produces architecture mistakes. The context window is the model's active attention space. Everything inside it is available; everything outside doesn't exist to the model, and it resets between calls unless your application manages continuity. Retrieval is external knowledge fetched at query time. It augments the window; it doesn't replace it, and the model only sees what the retriever surfaces. Persistent application state is owned by your system, not the model: order status, user records, balances. The model needs a tool call to get it. And summaries and memory layers are application-managed continuity across turns or sessions. The model has no native memory between calls, so anything that persists does so because your application stored it and passed it back. That's an architectural choice, not a model capability.

### Measure tokens, don't estimate them

The window is measured in tokens, and how much text a token covers varies by model generation, tokenizer and language. So treat any characters-per-token ratio as a rough illustration. Measure instead. Every API response reports actual token counts in its usage field, and those counts are what the limit and the bill apply to. Everything entering the window counts: the system prompt, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool outputs and the model's own responses. Remember the two edge errors from episode one: an oversized prompt is rejected with a 400 invalid request error, an oversized request body with a 413, and a prompt that fits but whose generation hits the ceiling comes back truncated with a model context window exceeded stop reason. Use the token-counting API before you send.

### Don't budget the full window

The practical rule is direct. Budget for the largest realistic conversation, plus retrieved context, plus system prompt, plus working scratch, plus margin for growth. The window is a ceiling, not a target. Designing toward the ceiling means you'll hit it in production. Module two adds the cost angle: model the token distribution, not the average. Most requests may be short, but a tail of long requests can consume most of the spend.

### The strategy spectrum

Every workload makes a choice about how context reaches the model on each call. At one pole is monolithic: everything in the prompt at once. It earns its place for bounded tasks with predictable input size, stable prefixes that benefit from caching, single-shot questions where retrieval latency isn't worth paying, and reasoning that genuinely needs simultaneous access to all the material. It breaks in conversations and tool loops, where context accumulates turn over turn. Cost and latency scale linearly with input length, and attention quality can degrade on very long contexts well before the hard limit.

At the other pole is progressive: carry forward only what the next step needs, retrieve just in time, summarise across turns. It's the right default for most production workloads: multi-turn dialogue, agent loops that depend mainly on recent state, and staged workflows with narrow handoffs. It breaks for tasks that need long-range coherence, for decisions depending on detail dropped earlier, and it makes caching harder when the carried-forward context mutates. It also means the exact input at step N isn't reconstructable, which complicates debugging.

Two strategies sit between the poles. Retrieval fetches relevant chunks from an external store: great for knowledge bases too large for the window, sources that change faster than you redeploy, and cases needing citations. It breaks on synthesis across many documents scored independently, on chunking that splits tables or code, and on recall failures where the right document never enters the top results. And retrieval quality becomes a system you must evaluate. Compaction periodically summarises accumulated context: good for long-running agents and phase transitions. It breaks when summaries drop load-bearing detail like identifiers, numbers or earlier decisions. The summariser is itself a model call, compaction is largely one-way, and measuring summary fidelity is an unsolved evaluation problem.

### Combining strategies

Production systems almost always combine these. The module's worked example is a long-running coding agent. At session start, a small, stable monolithic prefix with the task and referenced files, ideal for caching. During active work, progressive recent state, since each tool call appends what the next step needs. When the agent realises it needs a file it didn't load, just-in-time retrieval. And when early exploration fills the window, compaction that keeps what was tried and learned. No single strategy could carry that workload. So ask four separate questions. What does the model need at the start? That's your monolithic baseline. What does it need from recent steps? That's the progressive window. What might it fetch on demand? That's the retrieval layer. What can be compressed without losing decision-relevant detail? That's the compaction policy. And remember that context strategy and context sizing are separate decisions that interact. Treating them as one is where most designs go wrong.

### The silent budget killer

Module one's cost callout is a number worth remembering: a conversation that starts with a four-thousand-token prompt can be carrying eighty thousand tokens by turn thirty. Per-call cost grows with the conversation, and there's no visible signal until the bill arrives.

parts.narration:
### Why reuse is its own decision

Reusable prompts raise questions a one-off prompt never does. How do you reuse them efficiently, and how do you package them so a team can share and govern them? Module one answers with two tools: caching for efficiency, and the choice between a modular prompt library and a Skill for packaging.

### A cache that never hits

Start with the cautionary case. A team put a reusable analysis prompt into production and saw none of the savings caching should bring. The cause was ordering. They placed the per-request content, the document being analysed, at the top of the prompt, above the large fixed instruction block. The cache matches on a stable prefix, so putting dynamic content first meant the prefix changed on every request and the cache never hit. The fix was to reorder: fixed content first, dynamic content last.

### Caching mechanics an architect designs around

Four mechanics. Cache breakpoints: caching works on a stable prefix, so mark the boundary between the fixed, cacheable part and the variable part, and keep the fixed part genuinely fixed. Content ordering: static before dynamic, always. TTL selection: match the cache lifetime to how often the fixed content changes and how often the prompt is called. A prompt called constantly benefits from a longer-lived cache; one called rarely may never pay back the write. And the write overhead: writing to the cache has its own cost, so for a prompt called infrequently or with a small fixed portion, caching can cost more than it saves. Caching is a design decision, not a default.

Module two adds the operational details. Caching needs explicit cache control markers in the request. Cache writes cost more per token than standard input, so the cost model must include the write on first use. The default TTL is five minutes, so workloads whose requests arrive less often than that won't see consistent savings. Reads are much cheaper; the module illustrates ten percent of the input rate and tells you to confirm current pricing. And the response is identical with or without caching. What's stored is the processed prompt prefix, so there's one more risk: if cached content must reflect live state, caching creates a consistency window that may break the use case.

### Modular prompt library or Skill

There are two ways to make a prompt reusable across a team. A modular prompt library is a shared collection of fragments and templates that engineers assemble in their own code. A Skill is more formal: a versioned, self-contained unit, a SKILL dot M D file that packages the instructions, optional executable scripts and version management, so the procedure travels as one governed artifact.

Choose with three considerations. Repeatability: an assembled, often-tweaked prompt leans to a library; a stable procedure run the same way every time leans to a Skill. Distribution: shared within one codebase or team leans to a library; distributed across teams or products leans to a Skill. Governance: lightweight ownership of fragments leans to a library; a need for versioning, approval and rollback leans to a Skill, because Skills carry that. The risk on the other side is drift. An ungoverned prompt copied across teams becomes many slightly different versions, each with its own quietly different behaviour. Versioned reuse is the control.

### Skills as an integration mechanism

Skills aren't only packaging. Module one notes they're an integration mechanism. A Skill can be attached to a request through the container dot skills parameter, published and versioned through the v1 skills endpoint, and managed under version control like any deployed asset. Skills require the Code Execution Tool to run, so the integration carries a sandboxed execution dependency. When the question is how a reusable procedure reaches Claude across entry points, a versioned Skill is one mechanism to weigh alongside MCP and direct tool use. In Claude Code, Skills are also progressive by design: they're invoked on demand instead of loaded up front, which keeps the main context lean.

### Reuse at team scale

Module five takes reuse to the team. There are four ways to distribute a Skill: an org-provisioned Skill under organisation settings for everyone; a plugin assigned to a group, which gives install preferences, group targeting and version-controlled updates from a connected repository; a Claude Code project Skill that lives in the repository and versions with it; and an API Skill called by the partner's own products, with explicit version pinning. You'll go deeper on this in episode seven. The thread connecting all of it is the same: reuse is only safe when the reused thing has a version, an owner and a way back.

parts.narration:
### What capability bloat means

Capability bloat is what happens when an agent or tool-using system accumulates more tools and permissions than its job needs. It creeps in naturally. A team adds a tool for one edge case, another because it was easy to connect, a third because a previous project had it. Each addition looks harmless. Together they widen what the system can do, including combinations nobody tested.

Module one frames the risk precisely: an agent's autonomy is your liability surface. An agent can do anything its tools allow. The broader the tool permissions, the larger the space of things that can go wrong. Keep the tool entry point as narrow as the task allows. The reference-architecture table names the agent's characteristic failure the same way: unbounded autonomy, meaning state-changing tools with no human review, no turn limit, and no way to measure whether the goal was met.

### Least-privilege tool configuration

Module two turns this into an audit procedure. Every tool you connect to a Claude system is both an attack surface and a cost. Audit the tool set the same way you audit permissions. For each connected tool, ask whether it is essential to the task or merely convenient. Remove the ones that are out of scope, and record the justification for each removal. That last step matters, because it stops the tool from quietly returning, and it gives a reviewer the reasoning.

In an orchestrator-worker deployment, establish a trust hierarchy. Scope each subagent's tool access to its task, so a subagent can't reach tools its job doesn't require. A research subagent that reads documents doesn't need a send-email tool. A code-review subagent in Claude Code runs with read-only tools.

### Why bloat costs money and accuracy

Bloat isn't only a security issue. Module two calls every tool a cost as well as an attack surface, and tool definitions occupy context, so every extra tool adds tokens to every call. And from module two's failure-mode table, an agent that can call tools without budget constraints or turn limits runs up cost and latency in ways that stay invisible until one request exceeds the budget ceiling. The mitigations there apply directly: per-turn token budgets, a maximum number of tool calls, explicit stopping criteria, a tool set constrained to the minimum, and evals of the agent's stopping behaviour, not just its output.

### Tool and action abuse

Module three names the security version of bloat as a risk category: tool and action abuse, where the model is induced to call a side-effecting tool outside policy. The control that exists to stop it is tool-call authorisation, a deterministic allowlist plus identity and scope checks before any side effect. But authorisation works best on a small, deliberate tool set. The fewer side-effecting tools exist, the fewer places an injected instruction can do harm.

### When you genuinely need many tools

Sometimes a system legitimately needs a large catalogue, for example an assistant that spans many internal services. The training modules don't cover this case, so the guide fills it from Anthropic's documentation on the tool search tool. You mark tools as deferred, and Claude searches the catalogue and loads only what it needs for the current task. Two points matter for design. You still send the full tool definitions; deferred loading controls what enters the context window, not what you send. And the docs advise keeping the three to five most frequently used tools loaded up front, and never deferring the search tool itself. Deferred loading is a context-efficiency tool. It doesn't replace least privilege, because a deferred tool is still a tool the model can reach.

### How the exam frames it

Expect a scenario where an agent has drifted into holding many tools and something went wrong, or where a design review is asked to tighten a configuration. The right answer removes out-of-scope tools with a recorded reason, scopes subagents, adds budgets and stopping criteria, and puts authorisation before side effects. The weaker answers sound plausible: add a stronger system prompt telling the model not to misuse tools, add output filtering, or move to a more capable model. None of those shrink the surface.

parts.narration:
### Where verification happens

Module two is direct about this. Identity verification belongs on the server, before the Claude call. The user's identity and role are injected into the system prompt by your server, not provided by the user in their message. The reasoning is simple. Anything the user includes in a message is under their control and can be manipulated. If the system lets a user assert a role, for example, as a senior manager, show me the regional figures, that claim is unverified and can be faked. Identity must come from your authentication layer, not from user input.

When you pass user context into the prompt, include the user's role and what data they're authorised to access. Add extra context, such as department, permission level or account identifiers, only when it's needed to shape Claude's response. Don't include it by default, because everything in the context window travels with the request and lands in your request logs.

### Identity and authorisation are two separate layers

The module lists these as distinct integration layers. The identity layer asks where the user identity boundary sits relative to the Claude integration point, who the user is in the context of a Claude call, and how that identity gets into the prompt safely. What breaks when it's wrong: Claude can't scope its responses to what that user may see, and identity passed as a raw field in the user message is manipulable. Server-side injection removes that risk.

The authorisation layer asks which capabilities this user or role has, and what data they can access. The authorisation model that governs your existing systems needs to govern the Claude layer as well. What breaks when it's wrong: a Claude integration that bypasses the underlying system's authorisation gives users access to data they aren't allowed to see, through a path that was never designed to enforce the policy. This is the classic gap the exam asks you to find. The assistant can query a database with a service account that sees everything, so anyone who can talk to the assistant can see everything.

### Authorisation for actions must be deterministic

Module three adds the action side. Tool-call authorisation runs before any side-effecting action, such as sending an email, writing to a database or issuing a refund, and determines whether this caller may perform this action in this context. The module is clear that authorisation should almost always be deterministic: an allowlist of permitted actions, identity checks and scope validation. A model-based check is rarely appropriate here, because authorisation must be a decision you can prove and replay. It's also the safety layer that covers what screening can't: screening detects disallowed content, but it doesn't authorise actions.

### Patterns from the constraint matrix

Module two's constraint-to-integration matrix shows how identity works under real constraints. For attorney-client privilege, the API runs behind the firm's own application, through a firm-approved gateway that holds the API key, enforces who can access what, and produces an audit log the firm owns. Users sign in through SSO, and identity and permissions are assigned by the server and can't be claimed by the user. For HIPAA, users are verified through the partner's authentication system and access to protected health information is limited to the minimum necessary. For FedRAMP, users authenticate through the agency's approved identity provider and access is controlled by the agency's role and policy layer. For internal data-residency policy, users sign in through the partner's standard SSO with roles from existing policy. The common thread: the Claude layer inherits the enterprise's identity and authorisation, it doesn't invent a new one.

### Multi-tenant isolation

One more gap the exam likes. Module two warns that a multi-tenant system running on a shared API key can't attribute a rate-limit breach to the tenant that caused it. When the organisation-level limit trips at peak, the spike is visible but the source isn't, and every tenant absorbs the impact. Separate API keys per tenant are required for attribution and isolation in any production multi-tenant deployment. Pair that with server-injected tenant identity, so one tenant's data can't be requested by another.

### MCP authorisation

When tools are exposed over MCP, the same principle applies at the server boundary. The modules don't cover MCP's authorisation mechanics, so the guide fills that gap from the MCP authorisation specification. The architectural point is that an MCP server is a boundary where the caller's identity must be checked and its scope enforced. Don't assume a connector is safe because the client in front of it is authenticated.

### Reading a diagram for gaps

When a scenario shows an integration diagram, walk it in order. Where does identity come from: the server, or the message? Does the Claude path enforce the same authorisation as the underlying system, or does it use a broad service account? Is there a deterministic authorisation check before each side-effecting tool? Is there one API key shared across tenants? What sensitive fields enter the context window that the task doesn't need? Each yes in the wrong place is a gap, and the fix is almost always to move the control to the server side, into code.

parts.narration:
### The levers

Every configuration choice trades accuracy against latency and cost. Across modules one and two, the levers are the same handful. The model tier. Extended thinking, on or off. The context strategy and how much context you send, since cost and latency grow linearly with input length. How you retrieve. The output length cap, set with max tokens. And prompt caching, which cuts both cost and latency when a long, stable prefix is reused. The architect's job isn't to know every lever's exact value. It's to know which lever moves which budget.

### Latency is a distribution

Module two insists on the right latency metric. A demo usually runs one request at a time, and median latency under a single request is a different number from p95 under concurrent load. P95 is the latency below which ninety-five percent of requests complete; only the slowest five percent fall above it. SLA breaches and user abandonment come from that slow tail, so p95 is the more useful design target than the median. The same is true of cost: token distributions are skewed, and a model built on the average can underestimate cost by a factor of two or three.

### Two budgets, both binding

Module one's calculator sets the exercise. You pick a model tier, a context strategy, a daily call volume and extended thinking on or off, and you have to meet a cost ceiling and a latency budget at the same time. The two can't be traded against each other. Module two's calculator gives a concrete scenario: a customer service agent with fifty thousand requests a month, a five-thousand-token stable system prompt, three hundred tokens of input, four hundred of output, an eight-hundred-dollar monthly ceiling and a three-second p95 target. More than one valid configuration exists.

The model answer is the rule to remember. The dominant constraint depends on which budget is tighter. If latency is binding, the model tier and extended thinking are the load-bearing controls, because they most directly move latency. If cost is binding, the tier and the context strategy are load-bearing. The load-bearing control is the one tied to whichever budget has the least margin, and naming it explicitly is what makes the configuration defensible rather than lucky. In the module two scenario, a large stable system prompt also points straight at caching, and a max tokens cap protects both budgets from the long-output tail.

### The case that ties it together

Revisit the case from episode two through this lens. Ninety days after launch, cost was seven times the model and median latency was 2.3 seconds against an 800-millisecond target, with no satisfaction gain. Three things compounded: no model-tier decision existed at any step, so the default carried to deployment; cost was reviewed monthly, so the gap surfaced late; and extended thinking was on for a routing classifier that needed no reasoning. Here both budgets were blown, and the levers were tier and thinking. The team built an eval set per step, routed the classifier to Haiku, summarisation to Sonnet, and kept Opus only for final composition. Cost fell seventy-one percent, median latency reached 940 milliseconds, and satisfaction stayed flat, which proved the expensive configuration had bought nothing.

### Extended thinking as a latency lever

Extended thinking is the lever most often misused. Thinking tokens are billed as output and add latency on every call where thinking engages. Module one's rule is to run evals without it, work on the prompt, and enable it only for a measured accuracy gap. A routing classifier is the textbook case where it adds latency with no accuracy gain.

### Justifying the decision

When you present a configuration, say three things. Which budget is binding, and how much margin each has. Which control you moved, and why that control moves that budget. And what the eval showed per step, so nobody can say you traded accuracy away blindly. A configuration justified that way survives a design review. One justified as we picked the best model doesn't.

### Common traps

Expect distractors that move the wrong lever. Adding hybrid retrieval when the problem is latency from thinking. Upgrading the tier when cost is binding. Removing thinking everywhere when only one step needed it, which can drop accuracy where the eval showed thinking earned its place. And optimising the median when the SLA is defined at p95.

parts.narration:
### Why LLM observability is different

Module two opens with the core problem. An LLM-based system is harder to debug than traditional software because it doesn't crash when something goes wrong. It produces a subtly wrong response. Standard logging catches errors and timeouts. It doesn't catch an answer that's quietly incorrect in a way that has real business consequences. So observability for Claude has to be designed for silent wrongness, not just for outages.

### What to log on every request

The module names four things. The request: model version, input token count and prompt identifier. The response: output token count, latency and stop reason. The context: user role, session ID, and whether caching was applied. And the outcome: whether the downstream system accepted the output, and any rejection signals. That last one is the closest you get to ground truth in production. An acceptance signal from the system consuming the output tells you, at scale, whether outputs are being used.

### Four questions, four layers

Observability at scale has to answer four questions: what is the system doing, how well is it performing, when did it change, and why did it change? Each needs its own layer.

Request-level tracing is the raw material. Every request produces a trace with the model, model version, input and output tokens, latency, stop reason and any tool calls.

Metric aggregation turns traces into dashboard metrics: cost per request, latency p50 and p95, task success rate where the downstream system gives an acceptance signal, and error rate by error type. The critical warning is that aggregate metrics can look healthy while a small fraction of requests consumes most of the budget. Per-request decomposition is what protects you.

Anomaly detection sets threshold alerts on the metrics that matter. The module's examples: a cost spike above one hundred and fifty percent of the seven-day average deserves an alert, and so does p95 latency crossing the SLA. Model drift, a gradual change in the distribution of outputs over time, is harder to catch with thresholds and benefits from periodic distribution comparison.

Change attribution is the hardest layer. When a metric moves, the instrumentation should distinguish three causes. Model drift: the model's behaviour on stable inputs changed. Data drift: the input distribution changed. And model update effects: the model version changed and behaves differently on existing inputs. They have different fixes, and mixing them up produces the wrong one. You can only attribute a change if you logged the model version and can compare inputs over time.

### Observability across agents

In multi-agent systems, traces fragment across the orchestrator and its subagents. Module one's fix is a shared trace identifier propagated through every agent, so one run can be reconstructed end to end. Without it, you can't tell a recoverable subagent failure from an unrecoverable orchestrator one.

### Observability as the price of autonomy

Module two makes a point that matters for agent designs. Security organisations increasingly treat observability as the precondition for enabling agents at all. Without a trustworthy audit trail, an autonomous system isn't approved to act. Design for that standard. As a design-review item, verify which agentic actions are actually recorded in audit logs across your chosen surfaces, because coverage varies by surface, and an action that's taken but not logged is, to a security reviewer, an action that can't be allowed.

### Build it before the incident

Both cost callouts in module two say the same thing. Instrumentation added after the first production incident means the root-cause question can't be answered from the data you have. Building it correctly the first time is cheaper than reconstructing logs afterwards. And the risk callout: a system with aggregate-only metrics can look healthy while a small fraction of requests is consuming most of the budget and producing wrong outputs.

### Selecting a strategy

When an exam scenario asks you to choose a monitoring strategy, match the layer to the symptom. Can't explain a cost spike? You need per-request decomposition. Quality slid with no code change? You need distribution comparison and change attribution, with model version in every trace. A multi-agent run went wrong and nobody can say where? You need a shared trace ID. Security won't approve an agent? You need audit coverage of every agentic action. And in all cases, connect the technical metrics to the business metrics the sponsor tracks, which you'll see again in episode four.
