parts.narration:
### What a RAG pipeline is

Module one describes retrieval-augmented generation done well: a stable knowledge corpus, such as product manuals, internal docs or regulatory text, is chunked and indexed. When a question arrives, the most relevant chunks are retrieved and passed to the model as context. This part goes one level deeper into the pipeline: how the corpus is broken into chunks, how those chunks are indexed, and how the retrieval strategy is matched to the queries the system will see.

### Chunking: by what the corpus is

A chunk is the unit that gets retrieved. The module's rule is that the chunking approach is chosen by the structure of the source, not by a default size. There are three approaches.

Fixed-size chunking splits text into uniform spans, with overlap, regardless of structure. It earns its place on homogeneous, unstructured text where natural boundaries are weak, and it's the simplest to operate.

Semantic chunking splits on meaning boundaries: topic shifts and sentence groups that hang together. It fits prose where a retrieved chunk must be self-contained to answer well, and it reduces cuts in the middle of an idea.

Hierarchical chunking preserves document structure, sections and subsections, and retrieves at the level that fits. It fits structured documents like contracts, manuals and policies, where section context carries meaning. A clause pulled out of its section can mean something different.

### Indexing: by how queries are phrased

Indexing decides what similar means when a query arrives, and the strategy is chosen by the query pattern.

Dense indexing, with embeddings, matches semantic similarity, meaning rather than words. It suits queries phrased differently from the source: paraphrase, intent and concept matching.

Sparse indexing, keyword-based, for example BM25, matches exact terms: identifiers, codes and names. It suits queries that hinge on specific tokens, such as part numbers, statute citations or error codes.

Hybrid indexing uses both and combines the results. It's the common production case for mixed query patterns, and it recovers the exact-match results dense retrieval misses. When a hybrid index returns two ranked lists, they must be merged. Reciprocal rank fusion is the standard, low-tuning way to do it: each result is scored by its rank in each list, and the combined score favours items that rank well in both. The point for an architect is that combining dense and sparse results is a design decision with a known, defensible default.

### The trade-off you must state

Every retrieval design trades three things. Retrieval quality: does the right chunk come back? Latency: how long does retrieval add to each request? And maintenance: how much does the pipeline cost to keep correct as the corpus grows and changes? Smaller chunks and hybrid indexing tend to raise quality and latency together. Larger chunks and dense-only indexing lower latency and maintenance but miss exact-match queries. There's no universally right point, only the point that fits this corpus and these queries, stated as a trade-off you can defend. The cost callout adds: size the pipeline to the query patterns you actually have, not to the most thorough design imaginable.

### How RAG pipelines fail

Module two's failure table names the first thing that breaks in RAG: retrieval quality drift. It happens when documents are added or removed without reindexing, when query and document representations fall out of alignment, or when the index refresh schedule creates staleness for queries about live state. The mitigations: keep retrieval quality in the eval loop, monitor retrieval precision and recall as system metrics, not just output quality, and separate live-state queries from static knowledge queries. Module one's limits on retrieval add three more failure modes: synthesis across many documents the retriever scores independently, chunking that splits semantic units like tables, code or multi-paragraph arguments, and recall failures where the correct document never enters the top results.

### Measure what you can't see

The risk callout is the line to remember. The failure mode is a confident answer built on the wrong chunk. Retrieval quality isn't visible in the output; it has to be measured against a labelled set. That's why RAG design ties straight into evaluation: a labelled set of queries with the chunks that should come back, scored on every change to chunking, embeddings or index configuration. And complexity grows over time. A pipeline that was correct at launch can degrade silently as documents are added, so every chunking and indexing choice is something you'll maintain.

### Exam signals

If a scenario mentions part numbers, error codes or citations being missed, think sparse or hybrid. If it mentions answers that miss section context in contracts or policies, think hierarchical chunking. If it mentions quality sliding as the corpus grew, think retrieval drift and reindexing, monitored as a metric. And if the question is about current values like order status, it isn't a RAG pipeline problem at all, which is the next part.

parts.narration:
### The skill underneath: context engineering

Module one names the broader skill here as context engineering: deciding which mechanism is responsible for getting each kind of data in front of the model. Retrieval over a vector index is one mechanism. A tool call is another. Information placed directly in the prompt is a third. And application-managed memory is a fourth. Each fits a different shape of data. The most common reference-architecture mistake in the whole course is using retrieval where a tool call belongs.

### The retailer trace

Here's the trace the module uses. An electronics retailer's assistant gets, where's my order? Retrieval returns two chunks. The first, with a similarity of 0.78, says the order was placed on the eleventh of June and shipped on the twelfth by standard courier, with a tracking number. The second, at 0.74, says the order is being processed, with dispatch expected within twenty-four hours. The model answers: your order shipped on the twelfth of June.

Both chunks were real strings that existed in the corpus at different times. The index conflated them. In reality the order had shipped, been returned to the depot because of a damaged label, and was waiting for re-dispatch. That current state appeared in neither chunk, because an index captures what was true when it was written, not what is true now. And a customer service tool to fetch live order status existed in the partner's API. It wasn't called.

### What broke, and why

The module breaks it into four lessons. First, a category error. Retrieval is the right mechanism for knowledge: FAQs, policies, manuals. It's the wrong mechanism for transactional state. Second, it's a data-architecture failure, not a retrieval failure. Live state had been represented as historical text snapshots, so the system searched past snapshots instead of querying the system of record. Third, similarity is not truth. A higher similarity score means the text was semantically close to the query, not that it's current. Fourth, the fix is a tool call. Not a better chunker, not a shorter refresh interval, not a higher similarity threshold. The knowledge base keeps the FAQ content. The transactional database keeps the orders. Two kinds of data, two access patterns, two mechanisms.

### How to recognise it

The symptoms are distinctive: stale chunks, results that shift with each index refresh, and answers that contradict the database. A better embedding model or more frequent refresh won't fix it. And the risk callout explains why it's dangerous: the system looks healthy. Normal latency, no errors. There's no signal that anything is wrong until a user notices the answer doesn't match reality. The model returned a response, the response looked correct, and the customer got false information about their own order.

### Matching the mechanism to the data

Use module one's distinct terms as your decision tool. Reference knowledge that changes slowly, and that's too big for the prompt, goes to retrieval. A small, stable body of knowledge that every call needs can sit directly in the prompt, especially as a cached prefix. Persistent application state, such as order status, balances, inventory and ticket queues, is owned by your system, and the model reaches it only through a tool call. And continuity across turns or sessions is application-managed memory, stored by you and passed back in.

The feasibility lens from module two says the same thing from another angle. For the knowledge property, bring stable knowledge in with retrieval, fetch live-state data with tool calls, and flag uncertainty on contested claims.

### One assistant, two kinds of question

Many real assistants need both. The triage reference architecture shows how: classify the intent, then route documentation questions to knowledge retrieval, live-state queries like order status or account changes to a transactional API, and high-consequence actions to a human approval layer. Module two's RAG mitigation says the same: separate live-state queries from static knowledge queries.

### Exam signals

If a scenario says answers are fluent but contradict the database, or shift after each re-index, the answer is a tool call to the system of record. If it offers a shorter refresh interval, a better embedding model or a higher threshold, those are the traps. And if the data is a stable manual or policy set, retrieval is right, and the question is probably about chunking or indexing instead.

parts.narration:
### Keep the three layers separate

Module one insists on vocabulary before selection. Three terms are often used interchangeably, but they sit at different layers. The entry point is how a user reaches Claude: Claude dot A I, Claude Code, Claude Cowork, Claude in Chrome, Claude for Excel. It's chosen for the user and the work. The build-time interface is what engineers code against: the direct API, the SDKs, MCP and the Agent SDK. It's chosen for the engineering team and the integration. The delivery route is where API traffic terminates: the Anthropic first-party API, AWS Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI or Microsoft Foundry. It's chosen for cloud commitments and compliance posture. Every deployment involves all three, and a decision in one rarely dictates the others. Confusing them is the most common source of muddled architecture conversations.

### The build-time interfaces

The direct API is the HTTP interface. The team owns everything: retries, streaming, tool use, observability and the UI. Maximum control, maximum responsibility. The SDKs, in Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Ruby, C sharp and PHP, offer the same capability with language-native types and helpers for authentication, retries, streaming and tool-use plumbing. Any agent loop is still the partner's own code. The SDK is the default for embedding Claude in a product; you drop to raw HTTP only when a new API feature hasn't reached the SDK yet. MCP is an open protocol for exposing tools, prompts and resources from one server, so any MCP-aware client can discover and use them. It's a sharing convention across products, not a calling convention inside one. And the Agent SDK runs a managed agent loop, the same loop that powers Claude Code, from the partner's own application code. It handles iteration, tool execution and termination, in TypeScript and Python, at the cost of fine-grained control over each step.

### MCP versus API tool use

These are different layers, not alternatives. API tool use is how Claude calls a tool inside a single request. MCP is how a tool entry point is exposed and discovered across multiple clients, and under the hood an MCP server's tools are called through ordinary tool use. So the choice is about reuse. Pick MCP when one tool entry point must be reachable from several Claude clients, such as Claude dot A I, Claude Code and an internal app. Pick raw tool use when the tools live inside one product. Module two adds the trade-off: MCP keeps the integration layer separate from orchestration, but adds a protocol layer that makes debugging tool calls more complex than direct function calls. If only one client will ever use it, MCP is overhead without payback.

### Claude Code versus the Agent SDK

Claude Code is for developers doing real engineering work, in a terminal, IDE plugins, desktop or the web. Module two is explicit that it isn't a backend for multi-user or customer-facing products. Product integrations use the API, an SDK or the Agent SDK. The Agent SDK is the answer when Claude must act across multiple turns inside the partner's own product, with the partner's application controlling the workflow, and the Claude Code CLI is the wrong shape. The module's summary is the decision rule: one request, one response, use the API or SDK; reusable tools across clients, use MCP; multi-turn action inside your own product, use the Agent SDK.

### The bank case

Module one's case shows every mistake at once. A regional bank wanted an operations assistant for branch staff: look up balances, schedule appointments, answer policy questions. The proposal ran Claude Code on branch laptops with a CLAUDE dot M D file per branch, MCP servers for the customer database, appointments and policy corpus, and subagents doing compliance checks on every interaction. Three failures. The entry point was chosen before the user was named; branch staff don't run terminals. MCP was carried forward from a previous project; there were no other Claude clients in the bank to reuse those tools. And compliance, the highest-consequence path, ran on subagents, which give weaker deterministic guarantees than server-side code. The fitting architecture was a custom web app calling the API, authenticated through the bank's SSO, with compliance in deterministic server-side code and tool calls audited at the server boundary.

### Delivery routes

The delivery-route rule is about what the partner has already committed to, not capability; the model behaves the same on every route. A committed AWS agreement points to Bedrock, with IAM and spend under the existing contract. GCP points to Vertex AI, Azure to Foundry. The first-party API fits when there's no strong cloud preference, the partner wants new features as soon as they ship, or wants to keep AI spend with Anthropic. The trade-off: routes through a cloud provider tend to lag the first-party API on new features. Module four adds that multi-platform designs need an entry-point-responsibility map, saying which entry point owns which task and why, written before integration begins.

### Agent to agent: a source gap

The exam objective also names agent-to-agent connections. The modules cover only orchestrator-to-subagent delegation inside one system, and there's no Anthropic guidance on cross-system agent protocols in the supplied material. So treat this as a source gap. The inferred principle the guide uses is the same as for MCP: introduce a protocol between agents only when independent agents genuinely need to interoperate across system boundaries. Inside one system, the orchestrator and subagents with structured results are simpler and easier to audit.

parts.narration:
### The same spectrum, applied to capabilities

In episode two you saw the context strategy spectrum, from monolithic to progressive. This objective applies the same idea to capabilities as well as data. Monolithic means loading everything the system might need into the prompt up front: all instructions, all reference material, all tool definitions. Progressive discovery means staging it: loading only what the next step needs, and letting the system discover and pull in the rest when it becomes relevant.

### Why monolithic breaks

Module one is clear about where monolithic earns its place: bounded tasks with predictable input size, stable prefixes that benefit from caching, single-shot questions, and reasoning that needs simultaneous access to all the material. It's also clear about where it breaks. In conversations and tool loops, context accumulates turn over turn. Cost and latency scale linearly with input length. Attention quality can degrade on very long contexts well before the hard limit. And the window fills silently before anyone notices something has been truncated. Long-lived deployments built monolithically tend to degrade as the conversation accumulates. The cost callout gives the shape: a four-thousand-token prompt carrying eighty thousand tokens by turn thirty.

### Why progressive wins by default

Progressive context carries forward only what the next step needs. The module calls it the right default for most production workloads: multi-turn dialogue, agent loops that depend mainly on recent state, and workflows that break into stages with narrow handoffs. The glossary defines it as context, instructions or capabilities loaded in stages as the work needs them. That definition covers more than retrieved documents. It shows up in Skills that load reference files on demand, and in agents that gather information through tool calls instead of receiving everything in the first prompt.

### Progressive discovery in Claude Code

Module one's Claude Code layers give you concrete mechanisms. CLAUDE dot M D is the monolithic part on purpose: a file loaded at session start with standing instructions and conventions that apply to every task. Skills are the progressive part: markdown-defined procedures Claude Code invokes on demand rather than loading up front, which keeps the main context lean. Subagents add isolation: helpers with their own context window for bounded tasks like code review or codebase exploration that would otherwise clutter the main thread. Together, they're a small monolithic core with on-demand capabilities and isolated contexts.

### Progressive discovery of tools

The modules don't cover large tool catalogues, so the guide fills that from Anthropic's docs. The tool search tool lets you mark tools as deferred. Claude searches the catalogue and loads only what the current task needs. You still send full definitions; deferred loading controls what enters context. Keep the three to five most-used tools loaded, and never defer the search tool. Anthropic's engineering material on Agent Skills describes the same principle for Skills: only a short description is visible up front, and the full instructions and files load when needed.

### The trade-offs of progressive

Progressive isn't free. Module one lists its weak points. Tasks needing long-range coherence across the full history suffer. Decisions can depend on detail dropped in an earlier turn. Caching is harder when carried-forward context mutates each turn. And the exact input the model saw at step N is no longer easy to reconstruct, which complicates debugging. That last point connects to observability: if you stage context, log what was loaded at each step.

### Combine them deliberately

The answer is rarely all of one. The coding-agent example from episode two is the model: a small, stable monolithic prefix for caching, progressive recent state, just-in-time retrieval for things not preloaded, and compaction when early exploration fills the window. Ask the four questions: what's needed at the start, from recent steps, on demand, and what can be compressed? Context strategy and context sizing are separate decisions; treating them as one is where most designs go wrong.

### Exam signals

If a scenario describes cost growing turn over turn, accuracy falling as more instructions and tools were added, or a context window filling silently, think progressive discovery: Skills on demand, deferred tools, subagents for isolated work, and a small core. If it describes a bounded single-shot task with a large stable document that every call needs, monolithic with caching may be exactly right.

parts.narration:
### Why evals come before code

Module two opens with timing. The common approach is to build the system, see if it looks right, and test later. The module argues for the opposite: write the eval suite before production code. Doing so forces three things that are otherwise easy to postpone. You state what success means in measurable terms. You expose design assumptions early, when changing them is cheap. And you give yourself a gate that tells you whether a model swap, a prompt change or a new retrieval strategy actually improved the system. If you can't write an eval for a behaviour, you have no reliable way to know it's present, and every change you make is unverifiable.

### From business requirement to measurable threshold

A requirement like summarise claims accurately doesn't tell you what to measure. The module turns it into an eval criterion in four steps. First, identify the behaviour specifically: extract the filer's name, claim number, incident date and claimed amount from each document. Second, set the threshold. The module's example thresholds are one hundred percent accuracy on structured fields, a hallucination rate below two percent, and responses within schema ninety-nine and a half percent of the time. The crucial point is where those numbers come from: the business requirement, not whatever your first prototype happened to achieve. Third, identify the failure modes: a fabricated claim number, a missing incident date, a value taken from the wrong claim. Each failure mode becomes a category in your eval dataset. Fourth, include adversarial inputs: documents with missing fields, handwritten sections, unusual formatting and non-standard layouts. If your golden dataset has only clean inputs, your scores won't predict production.

### The five dimensions

The exam objective names five dimensions, and module two's exercise shows each one in practice. A regional insurer reads submitted claims, extracts claimant, policy number, loss amount and date of loss, summarises the narrative for an adjuster, and flags claims for possible fraud review. It must respond in seconds, stay within a per-claim cost, never leak one claimant's data into another's summary, and never auto-deny a claim.

Accuracy of field extraction uses a code-based eval: the expected values are known and verifiable by exact or schema match, so a function checks them against ground truth.

Latency uses a code-based eval: p95 is a number, and the check is whether it's under the target.

Safety needs two methods. Code for the deny action, because it's binary: either a denial was issued or it wasn't. An LLM judge for summary faithfulness, because whether the narrative represents the source claim without fabrication is an interpretive judgement a function can't encode.

Security, meaning no cross-claimant leakage, uses a code-based eval: scan each summary for identifiers that appear in any input claim other than the one being processed. It's deterministic.

Cost uses a code-based eval: cost per claim is derived from input tokens, output tokens, model tier and whether caching applies, and the check is whether it exceeds the ceiling.

Notice the pattern. Four of the five dimensions are checked in code. Only the interpretive part of safety needs a judge. That's the grading ladder in action, which is the next part.

### Useful metric vocabulary

The module's glossary gives you precise terms. Hallucination rate is the percentage of responses in which the model invented, inferred or stated information not supported by the input, the source data or the allowed logic. Structured fields are discrete data elements that must be populated in a defined format, like a name, invoice number, date, amount or policy ID, as opposed to free narrative. Schema is the required structure, types and allowed values of the output. And p95 is the latency below which ninety-five percent of requests complete.

### Don't forget the business metric

Module two also says a proof of concept gives you the first signal on whether the system moves the business metric it was designed to improve. Measure that outcome on your POC sample, even before you model production cost. A cost profile that fits the budget on a system that doesn't measurably improve the metric that matters is still a failed deployment. So your metric set has technical dimensions and at least one business outcome.

### Exam signals

If a scenario says the team will measure quality after launch, or set thresholds based on what the prototype achieved, the fix is evals before code with thresholds from the business. If it asks how to check a numeric or structural behaviour, the answer is code. If it asks how to check faithfulness, tone or reasoning, the answer is a calibrated judge.

parts.narration:
### The eval workflow

Module two lays out a five-stage workflow where each stage produces an artifact for the next. Stage one, define the task: state the behaviour in specific, measurable terms and write the prompt you'll use to test it. A vague definition produces a vague eval. Stage two, build the golden dataset: the inputs your system will meet, including edge cases and counterexamples, labelled with expected outputs. If it isn't representative, the scores aren't meaningful. Stage three, run automated checks: pass each prompt through the system and compare against the expected result. These are fast and cheap, for unambiguous behaviours like format compliance, schema validation and lookups against authoritative data. Stage four, score with a judge: for behaviours that need interpretation, such as tone, reasoning accuracy and edge-case appropriateness, a model-based judge assesses outputs at scale. Stage five, interpret and act: aggregate scores, but look per category. A change that raises the mean while quietly degrading edge cases or adversarial inputs doesn't make the system better.

### Three eval types

There are three ways to grade, with different speed and flexibility trade-offs. Code-based evals run deterministic checks in milliseconds and cost almost nothing: schema validation, regex, JSON parse, length checks, assertions against authoritative data. Their limit is that they can't judge interpretation. Model-based evals give a judge model the original prompt, the output and a rubric, and get back a score and reasoning. They cost roughly a model call per item, and judges can be inconsistent on borderline cases, which is hard to detect unless you force the judge to explain its score. Human review is for high-stakes or novel behaviours where neither code nor a judge can be trusted: safety-critical edge cases, new capability areas without rubrics, or outputs where a wrong grade carries real risk. It's also how you calibrate model-based evals. It's the slowest, most expensive and least scalable option, and humans bring their own inconsistency.

### The grading ladder

Pick the method by climbing a ladder. Use code wherever the behaviour allows it, because it never drifts. Use an LLM judge when the behaviour needs interpretation, and make it rigorous: detailed rubrics, constrained verdicts drawn from a small fixed set of labels instead of free-form scores, calibration against human-labelled examples, and a different model from the one being evaluated, to avoid self-preference. Use human grading as the last resort.

Judge calibration is the step many teams skip. A judge is itself a system that can be wrong. Before trusting it, run it on human-labelled outputs and confirm its agreement with human judgement is high enough. An uncalibrated judge produces confident scores that may mean nothing, which is worse than no automated grade because it seems trustworthy. And favour volume over perfection. Many automatically gradable cases beat a handful of hand-graded ones, because broad, cheap coverage catches more regressions and can run on every change.

### Datasets that represent production

Module one's downgrade case shows good dataset design: two hundred and fifty representative documents with hand-validated targets, stratified by document type, and sized so per-type scores stay meaningful. Stratification is what revealed that two types failed while the average looked acceptable.

### Multi-turn evals

A single-turn eval won't tell you how a system holds up across a conversation. Multi-turn evals are a separate category that score a sequence of exchanges. They check whether the system keeps prior context straight, whether it answers follow-ups without inventing things never said earlier, and whether quality holds as the conversation gets longer. Because the unit is a whole conversation, they need their own golden dataset: full transcripts with known good responses at each turn, covering the follow-ups, topic shifts and conversation lengths the system will see.

### Evals as the gate, and keeping them current

Every change, whether a model swap, a prompt revision, a context strategy change or a retrieval update, should run through the eval suite before it reaches production. The module's example: a team revised a summarisation prompt but didn't update the eval. Everything passed. Two days after release, multi-clause legal sentences were being truncated. The eval predated the change and didn't measure the behaviour that changed.

The postmortem case makes it vivid. A contract review assistant was tested by hand on ten contracts the team knew well, declared ready and shipped. Two weeks later it failed on contracts with non-standard obligation structures, pulling obligations from the wrong section. The eval suite existed, but it was built from those ten convenient contracts, not a representative sample, and when the prompt changed it kept passing because the golden answers still reflected the old prompt. Three decisions led there: convenient inputs instead of representative ones, no dataset update after the prompt change, and manual spot checks treated as a substitute for evals. Spot checks confirm one input produces one output; they can't tell you about inputs you didn't think of.

### Cost, complexity, risk

The module's callouts. Cost: every model-based eval is an API call, but don't let that shrink the eval below what the use case needs. Under-evaluating costs far more. Complexity: eval infrastructure is a parallel system to maintain: the dataset, the judge prompts and the thresholds. Risk: an out-of-date suite gives false confidence, and the highest-risk moment for a regression is when evals exist and are stale.

### Tests as gates in engineering workflows

Module five connects this to developer work. A regression test suite and an eval set turn correctness from a reviewer's judgement call into a gate that runs on every change. The checklist defines what must be true; tests and evals prove it repeatably.

parts.narration:
### Why LLM experiments are harder

Integration gets Claude into the stack. The next question is whether changes to it actually help. Module two treats A/B testing for Claude like any experiment, with one important difference: LLM outputs are probabilistic, so results are noisier and interaction effects are harder to control.

### The four components

A structured test needs four things, and the module says what goes wrong without each.

A hypothesis: a specific, falsifiable statement naming the treatment, the expected direction of the primary metric and any constraints on secondary metrics. The new prompt is better fails, because it names no treatment, metric or threshold. A usable version reads like: replacing the instruction to summarise with an instruction to extract the three most important action items will increase task success by at least five percent without degrading p95 latency. Without a hypothesis, any result can be read as a win, because you can always find some metric that moved the right way.

Treatment and control assignment: random assignment of requests to the new or current version, and consistent for a given user or session to avoid contamination. Non-random assignment makes the groups incomparable; if the treatment happened to get simpler queries, the win may be an artifact.

A primary metric, defined before the experiment runs: task success rate, cost per completion, p95 latency or a satisfaction proxy. Choosing it after seeing results is outcome shopping, and turns an experiment into a retrospective correlation.

A sample size calculated from the minimum detectable effect, the baseline value and the required confidence. LLM outputs vary more than deterministic systems, so the sample needs to be larger. An underpowered test can't tell a real effect from noise, and a team that runs until it sees what it wants will find it, real or not.

### Reading the result without overclaiming

Statistical significance means a result is unlikely to be chance at that sample size. Whether it's big enough to matter is a separate question; a significant change can still be too small to justify the cost of shipping and maintaining a new version. Before declaring a winner, ask two questions. Is the effect large enough to justify the operational overhead? And did any secondary metric degrade? A prompt that lifts task success while raising cost thirty percent may not be a net win, depending on the budget.

LLM experiments add one more failure mode: interaction between the treatment and specific input types. A change that helps typical inputs may hurt rare edge cases that barely appear in the test period but show up in a later seasonal spike. So aligning the test period and input distribution with real traffic matters more here than in most software.

### The 50-session winner that wasn't

The module's case: a support team ran a revised system-prompt instruction on fifty sessions and the old version on fifty. Task success was sixty-eight percent against sixty-two. They declared a winner and deployed. Two weeks later the new version had settled at sixty-one percent; the gain vanished. Three problems, any one enough to invalidate it. The sample was too small: a six-point difference on a high-variance metric needs hundreds per group. The input distribution wasn't controlled: the treatment group happened to get fewer edge cases. And the primary metric wasn't fixed in advance: they looked at task success because it moved the right way, and would have looked elsewhere if it hadn't.

### Shadow testing

A live A/B test sends real users to the new version, so a regression reaches some of them before the experiment closes. Shadow testing avoids that exposure. Run the new version in parallel, send it a copy of live requests, and serve every user the current version's response. Log the shadow outputs instead of returning them, and score them offline. The deployment decision is made before any user has seen the new version.

Choose between them by risk and traffic. Use a live A/B test when the deployment can absorb a small, bounded exposure to a worse version and traffic is high enough to reach a meaningful sample in a reasonable time; you get real downstream signals, like whether users accepted the answer. Use shadow testing when one bad output carries too much risk, or traffic is too low to support a live split before the change is needed. The cost is losing downstream signal, so scoring relies on an offline rubric or golden answers. In regulated deployments, where exposing users to an unvalidated change may not be allowed at all, shadow testing is often the only acceptable option.

### Planning the experiment

The module's experiment-design plane uses two axes: the expected effect size and the confidence you need before acting. A small expected effect with a high confidence requirement needs the largest sample and the most careful design. A large effect with a modest confidence need can be detected with a smaller sample. Placing a scenario on that plane tells you the posture and the minimum sample size.

### Iterating

Iteration means one change at a time, each tested against a pre-set hypothesis, with the eval suite as a gate before any live test. The cost callout says it plainly: without a pre-specified metric you'll always find a result you like, and an underpowered win leaves you maintaining a version no better than what it replaced.

parts.narration:
### Classify before you fix

Instrumentation tells you a metric moved. Diagnosis tells you what kind of failure moved it. Module two's advice is to classify the failure before attributing a change, because the common classes are distinct and call for different fixes. Teams that skip classification tend to try the fix they know, usually a prompt tweak, whatever the cause.

### The four failure classes

A prompt failure means the instruction was ambiguous or underspecified and the model filled the gap. The fix is in the prompt, not the model. This links straight to module one's underspecification: where the prompt is silent, the model improvises, differently each time. The fix is to make the implicit explicit: name the scope, the format and the constraints, and restate the goal.

A hallucination means the model produced confident, fluent content that isn't grounded in the input or a reliable source. The fix is grounding: retrieval, tool use or verification. The module is explicit that a stronger instruction won't resolve it. This is the next-token-prediction and knowledge properties showing up in production.

A model mismatch means the chosen tier is wrong for the task, or it was swapped without re-evaluation. The fix is model selection, gated by an eval. The classic signature is a system that worked on one tier and degraded after a cheaper swap, often in specific categories.

An orchestrator-workers failure appears in multi-agent systems. Trace across the orchestrator and its subagents. A recoverable subagent failure, which you retry or flag, looks different from an unrecoverable orchestrator failure. Attribution needs a trace that spans both.

### Change attribution

When a metric moves over time, module two adds three causes to separate. Model drift: behaviour on stable inputs changed. Data drift: the input distribution changed. Model update effects: the version changed and behaves differently on existing inputs. Each has a different mitigation. You can only tell them apart if your traces record the model version and you can compare input distributions over time.

### Symptom to cause to first action

Module five turns this into a runbook-style table, which is worth knowing almost word for word.

Output quality degraded gradually with no code change: the likely cause is a model or prompt change, or retrieval drift as the corpus grew. First action: compare against an eval set and check what changed in the model, prompt or corpus.

Latency spiked: context size grew, a tool got slow, or a cache stopped hitting. First action: use telemetry and traces to find the slowest span, check token counts per request and the slowest tool call, and confirm cache behaviour.

Intermittent tool failures: authorisation, rate limits, or an unhandled error path. First action: inspect the failing tool's auth and limits, and trace one failed call end to end.

Cost rose with no usage change: the model tier crept up, or caching regressed. First action: check the per-request model tier and cache hit rate against the budget model.

### Discernment

Module two names the competency behind good diagnosis: Discernment, the discipline of judging the quality of what the model produced rather than accepting it at face value. In production, that means classifying outputs as acceptable, needing revision, or needing override, and feeding that judgement back into evals and monitoring. A team without Discernment watches metrics move and never asks whether the outputs were actually good.

### Working an exam scenario

Exam diagnosis questions usually include a tempting wrong fix. If the symptom is fabricated details with no grounding in the source, the right move is grounding through retrieval, a tool or a verifier, not a firmer instruction. If quality dropped right after a tier change and only in certain categories, it's model mismatch: re-run the eval per category and consider partial routing. If outputs vary because the prompt never stated the format, it's a prompt failure. If a multi-agent run produced a confident but incomplete answer, trace across levels and check coverage. Say the class first, then the fix.

parts.narration:
### The POC-to-production gap

Your eval suite tells you whether the system behaves correctly. It says nothing about whether it can afford to behave correctly at the volume the partner expects. Module two calls this the POC-to-production gap, and it has four dimensions that are invisible in a demo: cost, latency, reliability and failure modes. A POC running ten to fifty requests a day produces a negligible bill. A demo runs one request at a time, so it shows median latency, not p95 under load. A POC has no retries or fallbacks, because a developer just refreshes. And a demo is tested on inputs the developer expected.

### Build the cost model before the architecture

Three inputs drive the model: call volume, the token budget per request, and the model tier. Module two's sizing steps make it concrete. Get call volume from the business owner, not from intuition or a sample dataset, including multi-turn continuation calls. Set the token budget as input tokens, meaning system prompt, retrieved context and user message, plus expected output tokens, and model the distribution rather than the average. Then project monthly cost: volume times input tokens at the input rate, plus volume times output tokens at the output rate, since input and output are priced differently on every tier. Use the cache read rate for cached input tokens. Compare the result to the ceiling, and if it's over, change the architecture before writing code. Finally, run sensitivity analysis: what if volume doubles, or the distribution shifts toward the tail?

### Why averages lie

Token distributions are usually skewed. Most requests are short, but a tail of long ones consumes a disproportionate share. A model built on averages can underestimate cost by a factor of two or three. The module's post-launch quotes make it real. One: raw demo costs presented without scaling to production volume, with error bounds, is where the risk lives. Two: we assumed the token distribution would be uniform; the long documents in the tail consumed eighty percent of total spend. Three: when the endpoint returned a 529 at peak on day three, the whole workflow went down, because the team had never tested what happened when a call failed. All three share a root cause: the POC was treated as a cost and reliability model, not a capability demonstration.

### The levers, in order

Per-step model tiering, validated by evals, is usually the biggest lever; the Opus-everywhere case cut cost seventy-one percent with no satisfaction change.

Prompt caching is the most effective lever when the system prompt is long and stable. It preserves the processed prefix so the API doesn't reprocess it. Savings scale with prefix length and reuse. Static content goes first, then the breakpoint, then dynamic content. It needs explicit cache control markers, writes cost more than standard input, reads are much cheaper, which the module illustrates as ten percent and says to verify, and the default TTL is five minutes, so infrequent workloads may not benefit. If cached content must reflect live state, caching creates a consistency window.

Context strategy: progressive instead of monolithic, with compaction for long sessions, because cost scales linearly with input.

The max tokens cap and output length, because output tokens are priced higher and long outputs add latency.

The Batch API for work that can run asynchronously. The module illustrates a fifty percent discount and up to a hundred thousand requests per batch and tells you to confirm the current figures. Model it as an alternative wherever the SLA allows asynchronous processing, and for regulated workloads check whether batch processing is covered by the BAA and compliance configuration before routing protected data through it.

Extended thinking only on a measured accuracy gap.

### Reliability is part of cost-performance

Optimisation isn't only about spend. Module two's reliability controls protect performance under failure: retries with exponential backoff close to the API call, circuit breakers at the service boundary, and fallback chains in the orchestration layer. A system with no fallback has one point of failure, the primary endpoint, and when it fails at peak the whole workflow fails instead of degrading.

### The exam's sample question

The exam guide's second sample question is in this territory: a large, stable instruction block called often, with a cost problem. The answer pattern is static first, breakpoint, dynamic last, and check that the call frequency actually makes caching pay.

### Traps

Optimising the average instead of the tail. Turning caching on where the prefix changes every call. Assuming a longer TTL fixes a prefix that keeps changing. Moving to a cheaper tier without a per-category eval. And presenting demo costs to a client without scaling them to production volume.

parts.narration:
### What monitoring must answer

Part 3.4 covered how to design observability at scale. This part is about running it: what you watch day to day, how it reaches the people who funded the system, and how a signal turns into action. The four questions still frame it: what is the system doing, how well is it performing, when did it change, and why did it change?

### The production dashboard

Module two's metric layer gives you the core dashboard. Cost per request. Latency at p50 and p95. Task success rate, where the downstream system provides an acceptance signal. And error rate by error type, because a spike in 429 rate limits needs a different response from a rise in 5xx server errors. Underneath sits per-request decomposition, because aggregate metrics can look healthy while a small fraction of requests consumes most of the budget and produces wrong answers.

### Alerts and distribution checks

Set threshold alerts on what matters. The module's examples: a cost spike above one hundred and fifty percent of the seven-day average, and p95 crossing the SLA threshold. Model drift is gradual and slips under thresholds, so compare output distributions periodically. And when something moves, attribute it to model drift, data drift or a model update, because each has a different fix.

### The translation layer

The people who funded the deployment aren't reading request traces. They read a KPI dashboard that tracks the outcome the system was meant to improve. So module two calls for a translation layer that connects technical metrics to business metrics. For a customer service agent, the business metrics might be average handle time, first-contact resolution and customer satisfaction. The observability stack measures latency, task success and error rate. The translation layer maps task success to first-contact resolution and latency to handle time, so the business owner can see whether the system moves their numbers. Build it at design time. Otherwise the first business review asks what's driving the change in handle time, and answering it means a retrospective reconstruction instead of a live query.

### Monitoring is not a feedback loop

Module four draws the line that the exam tests. A dashboard collects and displays signals. A feedback loop maps each signal to a trigger, an owner and a required action: signals, triage, decide, act, review. Its case lays an alert log beside a stakeholder review calendar over ninety days. Weeks one to three, everything is steady. Weeks four to seven, the eval score drifts down week after week, but the error rate stays flat, so no hard alert fires, and no review is held. Weeks eight to twelve, the score keeps falling and the stakeholder says output is less useful lately; the quarterly review finally surfaces it in week twelve. A quality-drift trigger should have escalated to an architect review by week five. Every signal existed. Nothing decided they mattered.

### Runbooks close the loop for the team

Module five tells the same story from the operations side. A support team watched dashboards stay green for a quarter while answer quality slid. The cause was a growing retrieval corpus the index hadn't kept pace with. The symptoms were visible the whole time, but the runbook entry, gradual quality decline with no code change points at the model, the prompt or retrieval drift, was missing. With it, a first-line engineer could have fixed it in an afternoon. So monitoring has three parts: instrumentation that collects the right signals, a governance table that turns them into triggers and owners, and runbooks that tell the owner what to do.

### Regulated monitoring

For regulated deployments, some reviews run on a schedule regardless of the metrics, such as periodic output audits against a documentation standard or scheduled residency confirmation. You'll see these in episode six's governance table. Monitoring design has to include them.

### Exam signals

If a scenario describes green dashboards and unhappy users, or a slow decline that no alert caught, the answer is a decision layer: a drift trigger with an owner and a runbook action. If it describes a sponsor who can't see value in technical metrics, the answer is the translation layer. If it describes a cost spike nobody can explain, the answer is per-request decomposition.

parts.narration:
### What the model's training covers, and what you own

Before adding controls, module three asks how much safe behaviour is already handled by the model. Anthropic trains Claude against a constitution, a written document describing the values and behaviour the model should show. The module notes the most recent published version is from January 2026. The constitution sets a priority order for when goals conflict: be broadly safe, be ethical, comply with guidelines, and be genuinely helpful. The ordering is holistic rather than strict. The result is that Claude arrives with a broad class of harmful output already reduced, before you write a single prompt.

But that layer is general by design. It doesn't know your partner's domain policy, data-handling rules or authorisation model. A request can fit Claude's general alignment and still violate a deployment rule, such as disclosing another customer's order. Claude can't enforce a rule it was never given. So there are two layers with distinct jobs. Training-time alignment lowers baseline risk. Inference-time control enforces your deployment's rules, through system instructions, input and output checks, tool permissions and human review gates.

### Four layers, each with a blind spot

The module stacks safety in four layers. Trained behaviour covers broad classes of harmful output on every request, but not your domain policy; Anthropic owns it. The system prompt covers role, tone and stated constraints inside a request, but not anything an adversarial input can talk Claude out of, because instructions are not enforcement; you own it. Runtime screening detects disallowed content on input and output, but it doesn't authorise side-effecting actions and can miss novel attacks; you own it. And authorisation decides whether a specific action is permitted for this caller in this context, but it doesn't judge content quality or fairness; you own it too.

The module's postmortem shows the silent failure. A team's internal assistant refused every harmful prompt in testing, so they assumed cross-business-unit disclosure was covered too, and never built an authorisation check. In production, a normal-looking request asked for a forbidden record, and Claude answered it. The rule they believed was enforced didn't exist in any layer.

### Three decision points on the request path

A guarded request path has three decision points. Input screening runs before the model call and decides whether the request should reach the model. Output screening runs before the response reaches the user and decides whether it's safe to return. Tool-call authorisation runs before any side-effecting action, like sending an email, writing to a database or issuing a refund, and decides whether this caller may do this here. They check different things at different points, so a control at one does nothing for the others.

### Model-based or deterministic

At input, use a model-based check when intent is ambiguous, like jailbreak or injection patterns rules can't capture, and a deterministic check when the rule is crisp: a blocklist, a regex, a length or format check. At output, use a judge model for qualities like toxicity or policy compliance, and a validator for known strings, forbidden fields or schema violations. For tool authorisation, almost always deterministic: an allowlist, identity checks and scope validation, because it must be provable and replayable. The two kinds fail differently. A model-based classifier can be evaded by clever phrasing. A deterministic rule is brittle: it blocks exactly what it was written for and misses the rest. So you chain them, knowing what each misses.

### The second injection vector

User-input screening catches instructions the user sends. It doesn't catch instructions embedded in content the system retrieves or receives from tools. In RAG, a malicious instruction in a retrieved document reaches the model after input screening has passed. In an agent, a tool response can carry instructions the model treats as authoritative. The module calls this the dominant injection vector in enterprise deployments with retrieval or tools, and the control is to screen retrieved content and tool outputs before they enter the context, with the same classifier you use on user input.

### Refusals from the API

When Anthropic's streaming classifiers intervene, the Messages API returns stop reason refusal, with a stop details object that the module says is available since Claude Opus 4.7. It carries a policy category and a readable explanation; both are null when the refusal doesn't map to a named category. As of the module's writing the categories include cyber, bio, frontier L L M and reasoning extraction, and it tells you to re-check the list rather than hard-code it. Your application should read the category and route refusal classes differently, tolerate an absent object on models that don't return it, and, once a refusal arrives, reset the context by removing or rephrasing the triggering turn, because continuing on the refused context returns more refusals.

### Fail open or fail closed

A guardrail you build can fail like any dependency: time out, error, become unreachable under load. Then it either passes traffic through unscreened, failing open, or blocks until healthy, failing closed. If you don't choose, the surrounding code usually chooses open. A guardrail that silently passes traffic is worse than one that blocks, because it gives the appearance of protection with none of the function. This applies only to operator-built components; Anthropic's built-in safety controls aren't operator-configurable and don't fail open. The full guarded path, then: user request, input screening set to fail closed, the model call, output screening set to fail closed, deterministic authorisation before any side effect, and every blocked or failed gate logged.

### The single output filter

The module's trace shows why one filter isn't enough. A customer service agent had an issue refund tool. No input screening was configured. The model emitted a tool call to issue a refund, the tool executed with no authorisation gate, and money moved. Only then did the output filter inspect the generated text, find nothing unsafe, and pass it. It sat downstream of the only action on the path that couldn't be undone.

### Skill supply-chain security

Skills are distributable code plus instructions, so they're a supply-chain risk: an untrusted Skill can carry logic that runs commands, reaches the network or touches files the moment it's invoked, invisible to your prompt screening. So audit before trust: read the bundle for anomalous calls such as network requests, shell execution, file access and credential reads, and for out-of-scope behaviour against its stated purpose. A formatting Skill that phones home is out of scope. Then confine it at runtime with least privilege in a sandbox, because a clean Skill can still fetch code at runtime. Allow Skills only from a vetted internal registry, verified publishers and signed releases. Don't assume the platform screens them for you. And record a verdict for every audit: approve, reject, or remediate and re-audit.

### Governing layers in Claude Code

Module one gives the Claude Code equivalents. Hooks are scripts on lifecycle events, used as deterministic gates the agent can't skip. Permission modes control what runs without prompting. And sandboxing contains the workspace with filesystem boundaries, network egress rules and constrained commands, so the environment enforces the boundary, not just the agent's judgement.

parts.narration:
### From controls to the threats they defend against

Part 5.1 placed the controls. This part asks what they defend against. Module three says an architect is expected to conduct and document a risk assessment for a proposed system as part of a security deliverable, and it gives you the categories to check every design against.

### The five recurring risk categories

Direct prompt injection: a user crafts input that overrides the system's instructions and redirects its behaviour.

Indirect prompt injection: malicious instructions arrive through retrieved content or tool outputs that the model treats as trusted, a vector that user-input screening doesn't catch.

Token-budget exhaustion: oversized or adversarially padded inputs consume the context or output budget, truncating work or inflating cost.

Tool and action abuse: the model is induced to call a side-effecting tool outside policy. That's exactly the failure tool-call authorisation exists to stop.

Data exposure: sensitive fields enter the context window or the logs where they shouldn't, creating a leak independent of model behaviour.

Notice that two of the five, token exhaustion and data exposure, aren't about the model misbehaving at all. They're about what the architecture lets in and what it writes down.

### Where to look: the vulnerability assessment

The module's method is to walk the request path and the data path together. At each entry point, user input, retrieved content, tool outputs, the model's own output, and the logs, ask what an adversary could do there and which control stands in the way. Anywhere there's a plausible attack and no control is a gap. This mirrors the guarded request path: input screening covers user input, content screening covers retrieved and tool content, output screening covers the model's output, authorisation covers actions, and data minimisation and redaction cover the logs.

### Limitations that aren't attacks

Risks also include the model's own limitations, which come from the four properties. Next-token prediction means fluent errors on specifics. Knowledge means stale or confident answers on rare or changing topics. Working memory means truncation at the window edge. Steerability means drift on abstract instructions or precise computation. And non-determinism means the same input can give different outputs, as in the reconciliation case, where a pipeline built as if it were deterministic produced a different categorisation for the same statement in week two and nobody noticed until an analyst re-ran a batch.

### Failure modes by architecture

Module two adds the failure each architecture shows first. Agents: unbounded tool use and growing context, mitigated by per-turn budgets, tool-call limits, stopping criteria and a minimal tool set. RAG: retrieval quality drift, mitigated by keeping retrieval quality in the eval loop and separating live-state queries. Document pipelines: no exception path for low-confidence extractions, mitigated by confidence scoring and a human queue. Orchestrator-workers: blurred failure boundaries, fragmented traces and dropped units at synthesis, mitigated by defined recoverable boundaries, a shared trace ID and coverage reconciliation. And from the POC gap: silent degradation, made-up outputs on edge inputs, or complete failure on an input class nobody tested.

### The risk assessment as a deliverable

The module is explicit that the assessment should be a written artifact. For each identified risk, record the category, the affected component, a likelihood-and-impact judgement, and the mitigating control, with an owner and an evidence artifact. That document is what the security reviewer signs off, and it feeds the compliance control register in part 5.4. A risk with no owner is a risk nobody is watching.

### Exam signals

If a scenario adds retrieval or tool use and asks what new risk appears, think indirect injection and content screening. If it mentions huge pasted inputs or runaway cost from adversarial padding, think token-budget exhaustion, with input limits and budgets. If it describes a model being talked into a refund or deletion, think tool abuse and deterministic authorisation. If sensitive fields appear in logs, think data exposure and redaction before the call. And if the question asks what the architect should produce, the answer is a written risk assessment with owners and evidence, not a verbal assurance.

parts.sources: [MODULE 3] Review routing – what sets the stakes; placement trade-offs; what the reviewer sees; consent fatigue and plan-level review; Diligence; When routing everything to review makes review meaningless · [MODULE 1] HITL checkpoint patterns for agent workflows · [MODULE 2] Low-confidence routing in document pipelines
parts.narration:
### Logging explains; routing prevents

Decision logging gives you a record of what each automated decision was based on. Module three makes the distinction sharp: a log explains decisions after the fact, but it doesn't decide which decisions a person should weigh in on before they take effect. A routing rule stops the wrong ones from taking effect at all. And the log you've already built is the raw material for what the reviewer sees.

### Review is a budget

Think of human review as a budget. You have finite reviewer attention, and you must spend it on the highest-stakes items. Three variables set where it goes. Reversibility: how easily a wrong decision can be undone. The cost of a wrong decision: what the mistake causes if it goes through uncorrected. Those two together set the stakes. A choice that's hard to reverse and expensive when wrong is high stakes regardless of how the system reached it. The third variable is confidence: the system's score for its own output. It doesn't change the stakes. It estimates how likely this output is to be wrong, which tells you how much of the volume should go to a person. And it's useful only if it's calibrated, because a model can be confidently wrong.

### The routing rule

Combine them into one rule. Route decisions to a person when they're low-confidence and either irreversible or high-cost. Let confident, reversible, low-cost decisions through. A confident, easily reversed, cheap decision can usually run without a human. A low-confidence, irreversible, expensive one almost always needs review. When the variables disagree, give more weight to cost and reversibility, because they decide the consequences, and let confidence decide how much of that high-stakes volume can go through unreviewed. And confirm that calibration; it's a task of its own.

### Where the human sits

Once a decision is routed, choose the placement. Earlier is safer and slower. Pre-action approval means the action can't take effect until a person approves it, so nothing irreversible happens unreviewed; but it adds latency to every routed decision and needs reviewer availability, so it doesn't scale to high volume. Post-action audit lets the action run immediately and reviews it afterwards, keeping throughput high; but the wrong action has already happened, so it suits only reversible, lower-cost decisions. Sampled review checks a fraction of decisions to monitor quality without slowing the process; but a bad decision can slip through unsampled, so it monitors the system rather than guarding individual outcomes.

### What the reviewer sees

A reviewer who can't see why an item reached them may approve without the judgement it needed. Give reviewers three things: the inputs that drove the decision, the model's output, and the reason it was flagged. Without the reason, they can't tell an edge case from routine traffic. Without the inputs, they can't tell if the output is right. What you put in front of the reviewer decides whether the review is real.

### Consent fatigue and plan-level review

The module cites Anthropic research on agent autonomy: requiring sign-off on every action adds friction without meaningful safety gain. A better approach is for a person to monitor what's happening and step in when needed. One Anthropic pattern reduces per-step approvals and moves review to higher-value checkpoints, like plan review or exception handling. Consent fatigue is what happens otherwise: asked to approve dozens of times in a row, reviewers start clicking through without reading. That's what led to plan-level review in Claude Code, where a person approves the plan, not each step.

### When routing everything makes review meaningless

The module's transcript is short and memorable. Reviewer: there are four hundred items in my queue today, same as yesterday. Lead: are you reading the inputs on each one? Reviewer: there's no way; I get the output and an approve button; I don't even see the inputs or why this landed with me; after the first hour I just hit approve to keep up. Two independent failures stacked. Volume: oversight that covers everything reviews nothing, so the fix is routing by stakes. Missing context: a reviewer with only an output and a button has nothing to check against, so the fix is showing inputs and the flag reason. Fixing only one still fails.

### Diligence and agent checkpoints

Diligence is the AI Fluency competency behind this: maintaining explicit human accountability checkpoints, noticing when automation pressure is eroding oversight, and auditing workflows for places where AI acts without review. For agents, the routing rule becomes a checkpoint pattern: place a gate before any irreversible or high-stakes action an agent would otherwise take, and sample lower-stakes actions instead of gating each one. Module two's document pipeline is the same idea in a workflow: low-confidence extractions go to a human queue instead of downstream.

parts.narration:
### Constraints eliminate options before preferences do

Module one sets the order. When a partner is subject to attorney-client privilege, HIPAA, GDPR, FedRAMP or an internal data-residency policy, those constraints rule entry points and routes in or out before cost, ergonomics or build effort enter the conversation. Name the governing constraint when you recommend an entry point, and let it eliminate options first. The API or SDK, behind a partner-approved gateway with logging, retention and identity controls in the partner's own infrastructure, is what survives most regulated reviews.

### The constraint table

Attorney-client privilege rules out consumer tiers of Claude dot A I for privileged review, and anything touching privileged material through a surface the firm can't audit end to end. Claude for Work adds admin controls and audit logs, but the firm must still confirm its configuration meets its privilege bar. What survives is the API or SDK behind the firm's application, with SSO, through a firm-approved gateway that logs every request.

HIPAA rules out any route without a Business Associate Agreement for the specific configuration in use. A BAA for one configuration doesn't extend to another, and beta features are generally excluded unless listed as eligible. What survives is the API or SDK on a BAA-covered configuration, via the route the partner already uses. Module two names the HIPAA-eligible paths: the Claude API directly with a signed BAA from Anthropic, AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI.

GDPR and data residency rule out routes where the execution region can't be pinned or data leaves the boundary at any step. What survives is a cloud route, Bedrock or Vertex, with the region pinned and DPA terms inherited from the cloud contract. Module two adds that the direct API's inference geo parameter currently supports us and global, not EU pinning. GDPR doesn't itself require EU residency, since cross-border transfers are lawful with a valid mechanism, but where a deployment has an EU residency requirement, use a cloud route. The module says Foundry EU residency was listed as coming in 2026 with no confirmed timeline, so verify before relying on it.

FedRAMP rules out anything not on an authorised environment at the required impact level. The eligible paths are Claude for Government for FedRAMP High civilian workloads, Bedrock GovCloud for FedRAMP High and DoD IL4 and IL5, and Vertex Assured Workloads for FedRAMP High and IL2. Claude Enterprise on the direct API isn't FedRAMP authorised. Authorised government environments lag commercial model releases, so confirm which model the route offers.

An internal residency policy rules out routes outside the approved vendor list, regardless of technical capability. That's procurement, not engineering: the right route is whichever one the CIO already cleared.

### Data handling inside the integration

Module two's PII case shows compliance failing after the route was right. A patient intake summariser sent name, date of birth, social security number, insurance ID, complaint, medications and allergies in the user message. The summary only needed concerns, medications and allergies. Thousands of log entries held social security numbers in plaintext. The fix was a server-side redaction step before the Claude call and a retrieval function supplying only the fields the task needed. Necessity is the filter: if the field isn't required for the language task, it doesn't go in the context window.

### Turning obligations into a control register

Module three takes the next step. Regulations state outcomes, not implementations. Each obligation becomes three things you own: a technical control that achieves the outcome, an owner accountable for it, and an evidence artifact that shows it's live. The evidence artifact is the one most often missed and the one the reviewer checks. Examples from the register: for HIPAA, use only a HIPAA-ready Enterprise plan or first-party API configuration under a signed BAA with HIPAA compliance enabled and only eligible features; evidence is the signed BAA, the admin setting and the eligible-feature list; owner, the security lead. For FedRAMP, an authorised route at the required level; evidence is the authorisation record and confirmation the workload runs only there; owner, the platform owner. For residency, regional processing and storage, with logs, caches, monitoring and retention checked; evidence is the residency configuration and a data-flow record; owner, the data owner. For transparency, decision logging retained and queryable; evidence is a sample reconstruction from the live log; owner, the architect.

### Training use versus retention

Keep two claims apart. Data may be excluded from model training by default while still being retained or monitored for logging, abuse prevention, legal compliance or configured audit purposes. Module two adds that Anthropic doesn't retain API conversation content by default beyond what's technically necessary, but specific carve-outs exist, and your own application logs still capture whatever you send.

### Passing the filter is not finishing compliance

The module's case: a team chose a compliant route for a regulated workload and treated compliance as done. Obligations were mapped to controls once, in a design document, with no owners and no logging to show any control operating. Months later a logging change began writing request metadata to a store in a second region. Nothing caught it, because nobody owned the residency control and no artifact tracked where data landed. The audit asked for evidence that data stayed in-region, and the team had a design document. Configurations drift, so the register is revalidated on a regular cadence.

parts.narration:
### The failure runtime controls can't see

Runtime controls stop disallowed outputs from leaving the system. Module three points out what they miss: an output that passes every check but produces different outcomes for different people. That's harder to detect and harder to attribute, because on the surface it looks like a normal output.

### Fairness enters at identifiable points

The module's key move is to stop treating fairness as a single property of the model and start treating it as something that enters at specific points you can inspect. In a Claude system there are four. The retrieval corpus can over-represent or under-represent groups, so the context the model sees is already skewed. The framing of the prompt can encode an assumption that pushes outcomes one way. The examples used in few-shot prompting can carry the same skew as the corpus. And the downstream routing, what happens to the output after it's produced, can send some groups down different paths. Each is an injection point you can instrument, which is what makes fairness an architectural property. Module one's prompting guidance covers two of these from the construction side: phrase neutrally and balance examples across the cases the system will see, because bias in a prompt is invisible in any one output and only shows up in aggregate.

### Who asks determines what the system explains

Three audiences need explanations, and each needs a different slice. An affected user needs a clear explanation of why a decision affecting them was made, in terms they can act on; you need to capture the inputs that drove it and the reason. A regulator needs evidence that comparable cases are treated consistently and that a specific decision can be reconstructed on demand; you need a durable, queryable record of inputs, outputs and decision path. Your build team needs enough detail to find why a flagged decision went wrong; you need the full trace: prompt, retrieved context, model output and every routing step.

### Decision logging

To replay and explain one decision, capture the inputs, the retrieved context, the model output and the routing it went through. The module notes this is the same observability instrumentation from production work, pointed at a different question. Instead of asking whether the system is healthy, you're asking why a specific decision happened. The instrumentation is the same; the retention and the query path differ.

### The checklist

The module applies a checklist to a credit-decision support system. Which of the four injection points could skew this outcome, and is each instrumented? For an adverse decision, can you produce the inputs and the reason in terms the applicant can act on? If a regulator asks whether similar applicants were treated comparably, can you query the log and answer? Can your team pull the full trace for any flagged decision? A no anywhere is a design gap.

### Discernment

Discernment, evaluating AI outputs and behaviours, is the competency here. In practice it means judging whether an output is acceptable, needs revision, or needs override, instead of only confirming a value was produced. Applied to fairness, Discernment is what lets a reviewer recognise a skewed or unjustified outcome. A transparency record is what makes that recognition possible.

### When fairness is treated as the vendor's problem

The module's post-incident review is a single quote: we assumed fairness was the model's job; the skew was in our retrieval corpus, and we had logged so little that we couldn't prove it. The model had passed its vendor fairness evaluations. The unequal outcomes came from a corpus that over-represented some cases, an injection point the team never monitored because they'd assigned fairness to the vendor. When outcomes were questioned, there was no decision-level log, so they could neither explain specific decisions nor rule out the corpus, and couldn't answer the one question the regulator asked: where did the skew come from?

### Governing the log itself

The decision log is in scope for the compliance register. In HIPAA or GDPR contexts, logged inputs and retrieved context contain sensitive personal data. Apply minimisation, retention limits and access controls to it, and map it as a named control. Logging for transparency and minimising for compliance aren't in conflict; they need the same log, governed differently. And watch the aggregate trap: an outcome metric can look fine overall while harm concentrates in one subgroup. Measure by subgroup where the decision affects people.

### Exam signals

If a scenario says the model passed the vendor's bias evaluations but outcomes are still unequal, look at the corpus, the prompt framing, the examples and the routing. If a regulator asks for a reconstruction and the team can't produce one, the missing piece is decision logging. If an applicant must be told why they were denied, the system needs the inputs and reason captured in actionable terms.
